## 0–9

<a id="128b-130b-encoding"></a>**128b/130b encoding** — The PCIe 3.0–5.0 line code: a 2-bit sync header in front of 128 scrambled bits, 98.5% efficient against 8b/10b's 80%, relying on the scrambler rather than the code for transitions and DC balance. *First defined in* [24-05](../courses/24-high-speed-io-signal-integrity-and-photonics/chapters/24-05-pcie-cxl-ethernet.md). *See also:* [PCI Express (PCIe)](#pci-express-pcie).

<a id="1t1c-cell"></a>**1T1C cell** — The DRAM bit cell: one access transistor gated by the wordline and one storage capacitor; the bit is the capacitor's charge, read by sharing it with the bitline. *First defined in* [23-03](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-03-dram-cells-arrays-refresh.md). *See also:* [Storage capacitance](#storage-capacitance), [Charge sharing](#charge-sharing).

<a id="2-5d-integration"></a>**2.5D integration** — Placing several dies side by side on a layer of wiring much finer than a package substrate (a silicon or RDL interposer, or silicon bridges), so they can exchange thousands of short signals. *First defined in* [25-07](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-07-advanced-packaging-and-chiplets.md). *See also:* [Silicon interposer](#silicon-interposer), [RDL interposer](#rdl-interposer), [Silicon bridge (EMIB, LSI)](#silicon-bridge-emib-lsi).

<a id="3d-integration"></a>**3D integration** — Stacking dies on top of each other and connecting them vertically through TSVs, microbumps or hybrid bonds, for the shortest and densest die-to-die connections at the cost of heat removal and test access. *First defined in* [25-07](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-07-advanced-packaging-and-chiplets.md). *See also:* [Through-silicon via (TSV)](#through-silicon-via-tsv), [Hybrid bonding](#hybrid-bonding).

<a id="3d-nand"></a>**3D NAND** — NAND flash built as vertical strings through a stack of hundreds of wordline layers, so density grows with layer count rather than lithographic shrink. *First defined in* [23-06](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-06-nand-flash-and-3d-nand.md). *See also:* [Channel hole](#channel-hole), [Charge-trap flash](#charge-trap-flash).

<a id="6f-cell"></a>**6F² cell** — Today's DRAM cell footprint, 3F × 2F where F is the half-pitch design rule, with one bitline contact shared by two cells; 4F² cells with vertical-channel transistors would cut it by a third. *First defined in* [23-03](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-03-dram-cells-arrays-refresh.md). *See also:* [1T1C cell](#1t1c-cell).

<a id="letter-a"></a>

## A

<a id="a-stability"></a>**A-stability** — The property that a numerical integrator is stable for every decaying mode (Re hλ < 0) at any step size; backward Euler and the trapezoidal rule are A-stable, explicit methods never are. *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md). *See also:* [Stiff system](#stiff-system).

<a id="a-b-update"></a>**A/B update** — A firmware-update scheme with two executable slots: the new image is written to the inactive slot and the bootloader starts the newest valid one, so no copy is needed and the other slot remains for rollback. *First defined in* [18-08](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-08-boot-and-firmware-update.md). *See also:* [Image swap](#image-swap), [Rollback](#rollback).

<a id="abcd-parameters"></a>**ABCD parameters** — Transmission parameters, V1 = A V2 − B I2 and I1 = C V2 − D I2, chosen so that cascaded two-ports multiply; a series impedance is [[1, Z], [0, 1]], a shunt admittance [[1, 0], [Y, 1]], and AD − BC = 1 for a reciprocal network. *First defined in* [07-10](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-10-two-port-networks.md). *See also:* [Two-port network](#two-port-network).

<a id="absolute-summability"></a>**Absolute summability** — The condition Σ|h[n]| < ∞ (or ∫|h(t)| dt < ∞) on an impulse response, necessary and sufficient for BIBO stability of an LTI system; the sum is also the system's worst-case gain for bounded inputs. *First defined in* [11-03](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-03-convolution.md). *See also:* [BIBO stability](#bibo-stability).

<a id="absorption-coefficient"></a>**Absorption coefficient** — The rate α at which light intensity decays with depth in a material, I ∝ e^(−αx); 1/α is the penetration depth, and direct-gap materials have large α just above the gap. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="abstraction"></a>**Abstraction** — A simplified description of a system level that exposes a contract (inputs, outputs, assumptions) and hides internal detail, so that the level above can be designed without the detail. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="ac-analysis"></a>**AC analysis** — A simulation of a circuit's small-signal sinusoidal response versus frequency, computed with phasors after linearizing around the operating point. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="ac-analysis-spice"></a>**AC analysis (SPICE)** — A simulator analysis that linearizes the circuit at its DC operating point and solves its complex nodal equations at each frequency of a sweep, giving phasors; it ignores nonlinearity, clipping and transients. *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="ac-bridge"></a>**AC bridge** — A four-arm bridge driven by a sinusoid whose detector nulls when Z₁Z₄ = Z₂Z₃; being one complex equation, balance gives two real conditions, such as an unknown inductance and its resistance (Maxwell bridge). *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="accelerated-life-test"></a>**Accelerated life test** — A test at elevated stress (temperature, voltage, humidity) that makes failures occur sooner, with an acceleration model used to translate results to use conditions. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="acceleration-factor"></a>**Acceleration factor** — The ratio of a failure mechanism's lifetime at use conditions to its lifetime at stress conditions, the product of thermal (Arrhenius), voltage, current or field factors; it converts accelerated-test results into field predictions. *First defined in* [25-09](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-09-reliability-physics.md). *See also:* [Activation energy](#activation-energy), [HTOL](#htol).

<a id="acceptor"></a>**Acceptor** — An impurity with one fewer valence electron than the atom it replaces (B, Al, Ga or In in silicon), which captures an electron from the valence band, leaving a mobile hole and making the material p-type. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md). *See also:* [Donor](#donor).

<a id="access-granularity"></a>**Access granularity** — The bytes a memory channel moves per access, width times burst length divided by eight; DDR systems hold it at one 64-byte cache line. *First defined in* [23-04](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-04-dram-interfaces.md). *See also:* [DDR5 subchannel](#ddr5-subchannel).

<a id="accumulation"></a>**Accumulation** — The MOS bias regime in which majority carriers crowd to the surface (gate below flat band for p-type), so the capacitor behaves like a simple parallel-plate capacitor, C ≈ C_ox. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="accumulation-function"></a>**Accumulation function** — A(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt, the running total of f from a fixed start; for a current it is the charge delivered so far. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="acoustic-wave-filter"></a>**Acoustic wave filter** — A filter whose resonators store energy as sound waves in a piezoelectric crystal, tens of thousands of times slower than light, so that gigahertz resonators are micrometres in size with Q in the thousands; the basis of almost every cellular duplexer. *First defined in* [21-09](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-09-rf-front-end.md). *See also:* [Surface acoustic wave (SAW) filter](#surface-acoustic-wave-saw-filter), [Bulk acoustic wave (BAW) resonator](#bulk-acoustic-wave-baw-resonator).

<a id="acquisition-time"></a>**Acquisition time** — The time a sampling ADC connects its sample capacitor to the input; it must cover about (N + 1) ln 2 time constants of the source and switch resistance with the capacitor for N-bit settling. *First defined in* [18-06](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-06-adc-dac-pwm.md). *See also:* [Sample-and-hold](#sample-and-hold).

<a id="activation-energy"></a>**Activation energy** — The energy barrier E_a of a thermally activated process; it sets how strongly temperature accelerates the process through the Arrhenius factor exp(−E_a/kT), and each failure mechanism has its own value. *First defined in* [25-09](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-09-reliability-physics.md). *See also:* [Arrhenius model](#arrhenius-model), [Acceleration factor](#acceleration-factor).

<a id="activation-energy-dram"></a>**Activation energy (DRAM)** — The energy to open a DRAM row: sensing and restoring every bit in it, typically a kilobyte, whether or not those bits are then read; divided by the bits actually used, it rewards row-buffer locality. *First defined in* [23-01](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-01-memory-hierarchy-and-memory-wall.md).

<a id="active-clamp"></a>**Active clamp** — A second switch and capacitor that absorb a converter's leakage energy and return it instead of burning it, often also enabling zero-voltage switching. *First defined in* [22-04](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-04-isolated-converters.md). *See also:* [RCD clamp](#rcd-clamp).

<a id="active-load"></a>**Active load** — A transistor current source used in place of a load resistor, giving a large small-signal resistance (its r_o) while consuming little DC headroom; a common-source stage with an active load approaches gain g_m(r_o1 ∥ r_o2). *First defined in* [10-06](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-06-mos-single-stage-amplifiers.md).

<a id="active-noise-cancellation-anc"></a>**Active noise cancellation (ANC)** — Playing an inverted copy of measured noise so that it cancels at the ear; the delay of the anti-noise path limits cancellation to frequencies where 2 sin(pi f tau) is small, and gain mismatch limits its depth. *First defined in* [27-04](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-04-wearables-earbuds-and-glasses.md). *See also:* [Driver sensitivity](#driver-sensitivity).

<a id="activity-factor"></a>**Activity factor** — α, the fraction of clock cycles in which a node makes a 0→1 transition; it scales the dynamic power αCV²f. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="adaptive-data-rate-adr"></a>**Adaptive data rate (ADR)** — LoRaWAN's mechanism by which the network assigns each device the fastest spreading factor and lowest transmit power its link margin allows, minimizing airtime and energy. *First defined in* [27-08](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-08-edge-ai-and-iot.md). *See also:* [Spreading factor (LoRa)](#spreading-factor-lora).

<a id="adaptive-voltage-scaling-avs"></a>**Adaptive voltage scaling (AVS)** — Setting each chip's supply from measurements of that chip (ring oscillators, critical-path monitors) rather than a worst-case table, removing guardband; dynamic power falls as the square of the voltage reduction ratio. *First defined in* [22-08](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-08-pmics.md). *See also:* [Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)](#dynamic-voltage-and-frequency-scaling-dvfs), [AVSBus](#avsbus).

<a id="adiabatic-charging"></a>**Adiabatic charging** — Charging a capacitor with a slowly ramped or stepped source so that the voltage across the series resistance stays small, reducing the loss below ½CV² (to CV²/2N for N equal steps). *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="adjacent-channel-leakage-ratio-aclr"></a>**Adjacent-channel leakage ratio (ACLR)** — The power a transmitter leaks into the neighbouring channel relative to its in-channel power; for a cubic nonlinearity and a noise-like signal, (P/P_IIP3)²/3, i.e. 2(P_in − IIP3) − 4.77 dB. *First defined in* [21-07](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-07-power-amplifiers.md). *See also:* [Third-order intercept point (IP3)](#third-order-intercept-point-ip3).

<a id="admittance"></a>**Admittance** — Y = 1/Z = G + jB (siemens), the ratio of current phasor to voltage phasor; admittances in parallel add. Its real part, the conductance G = R/(R² + X²), is not 1/R unless the reactance is zero. *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md). *See also:* [Impedance](#impedance), [Susceptance](#susceptance).

<a id="aec-q100"></a>**AEC-Q100** — The Automotive Electronics Council's stress-test qualification standard for integrated circuits, with temperature grades defined as ambient ranges from Grade 3 (−40 to +85 °C) to Grade 0 (−40 to +150 °C); revision J dates from August 2023. *First defined in* [25-10](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-10-qualification-and-functional-safety.md). *See also:* [Qualification](#qualification).

<a id="affinity-laws"></a>**Affinity laws** — For fans and centrifugal pumps, flow scales with speed, pressure with speed squared and power with speed cubed, which is why variable-speed drives save so much energy on them. *First defined in* [22-11](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-11-electric-machines.md).

<a id="agile-development"></a>**Agile development** — Iterative development in short cycles (sprints) that each deliver working software, with continuous customer feedback and adaptation to changing requirements (Agile Manifesto, 2001). *First defined in* [05-09](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-09-software-engineering-practices.md).

<a id="air-gap"></a>**Air gap** — A deliberate break in a magnetic core's flux path, usually a fraction of a millimetre, whose reluctance dominates the core's; it sets the inductance by geometry and stores most of an inductor's energy. *First defined in* [22-05](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-05-magnetics-design.md). *See also:* [Reluctance](#reluctance), [Fringing flux](#fringing-flux).

<a id="alamouti-code"></a>**Alamouti code** — A space-time block code for two transmit antennas that sends (s1, s2) then (−s2\*, s1\*), letting a linear receiver separate both symbols with full diversity order 2 at rate one, 3 dB below receive MRC, without channel knowledge at the transmitter. *First defined in* [17-11](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-11-mimo-and-beamforming.md). *See also:* [Diversity order](#diversity-order), [Maximal-ratio combining](#maximal-ratio-combining).

<a id="aliasing-predictor"></a>**Aliasing (predictor)** — Two branches sharing a predictor entry because their indexes coincide; usually destructive when their behaviour differs. *First defined in* [14-07](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md).

<a id="aliasing-programming"></a>**Aliasing (programming)** — Two or more names referring to the same object, so a change made through one is visible through the others; assignment in Python never copies. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="aliasing-sampling"></a>**Aliasing (sampling)** — The folding of frequencies above half the sample rate onto lower ones, because tones differing by a multiple of f_s give identical samples; a tone at f₀ appears at |f₀ − kf_s| ≤ f_s/2, and aliased signal or noise cannot be separated after sampling. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Anti-aliasing filter](#anti-aliasing-filter), [Sampling theorem](#sampling-theorem).

<a id="all-digital-pll-adpll"></a>**All-digital PLL (ADPLL)** — A PLL built from a time-to-digital converter, a digital loop filter and a digitally controlled oscillator instead of a charge pump, analog filter and VCO; its dynamics are set by digital coefficients. *First defined in* [20-10](../courses/20-analog-and-mixed-signal-ic-design/chapters/20-10-plls-and-jitter.md). *See also:* [Time-to-digital converter (TDC)](#time-to-digital-converter-tdc).

<a id="all-pass-filter"></a>**All-pass filter** — A circuit with |H(jω)| = 1 at all frequencies but a frequency-dependent phase, such as (1 − jωRC)/(1 + jωRC) with phase −2 arctan(ωRC); it changes a waveform's shape without changing its amplitude spectrum. In discrete time (16-02): |H(e^(jω))| = 1, built from poles at p and zeros at 1/p\*, for example (z⁻¹ − a)/(1 − az⁻¹), whose group delay is positive at every frequency. *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="all-reduce"></a>**All-reduce** — A collective operation that leaves every one of p devices holding the elementwise sum (or average) of all their vectors; it synchronizes gradients in data-parallel training. *First defined in* [27-07](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-07-ai-datacenter-server-and-rack.md). *See also:* [Ring all-reduce](#ring-all-reduce), [Hierarchical all-reduce](#hierarchical-all-reduce).

<a id="aloha"></a>**ALOHA** — Random access in which users transmit whenever they have data and retransmit after collisions; throughput peaks at 1/(2e) ≈ 0.184 (pure) or 1/e ≈ 0.368 (slotted) of the channel. *First defined in* [17-12](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-12-multiple-access-and-cellular-wifi.md). *See also:* [CSMA/CA](#csma-ca).

<a id="alpha-power-law"></a>**Alpha-power law** — Sakurai and Newton's model of a short-channel MOSFET's saturation current, I = (K/2)(V_GS − V_TH)^α, with α = 2 for the square law and α approaching 1 under full velocity saturation. *First defined in* [19-01](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-01-cmos-inverter-static.md). *See also:* [Velocity saturation](#velocity-saturation).

<a id="alternation-theorem"></a>**Alternation theorem** — A linear-phase FIR approximation with L + 1 free cosine coefficients is the unique minimax solution if and only if its weighted error reaches its maximum magnitude, with alternating signs, at no fewer than L + 2 frequencies. *First defined in* [16-06](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-06-fir-filter-design.md). *See also:* [Equiripple filter](#equiripple-filter).

<a id="always-on-display-aod"></a>**Always-on display (AOD)** — A display mode that keeps a dim, mostly dark watch or phone face visible at all times, made affordable by OLED emission proportional to lit area and by refresh rates near 1 Hz. *First defined in* [27-03](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-03-wearables-smartwatch.md). *See also:* [Average pixel level (APL)](#average-pixel-level-apl), [LTPO backplane](#ltpo-backplane).

<a id="always-on-domain"></a>**Always-on domain** — The small part of a chip that stays powered in every mode: a low-frequency oscillator and real-time clock, wake-up logic and a few backup registers. *First defined in* [18-09](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-09-ultra-low-power-design.md). *See also:* [Power mode](#power-mode).

<a id="always-on-floor"></a>**Always-on floor** — The power a battery device draws when the user does nothing and the display is off, the sum of the application processor's sleep state, background wakes, the always-on domain, radio link maintenance, controller scanning, converter quiescent currents and leakage. *First defined in* [27-03](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-03-wearables-smartwatch.md). *See also:* [Always-on domain](#always-on-domain), [Quiescent current](#quiescent-current).

<a id="am-pm-conversion"></a>**AM-PM conversion** — The change of an amplifier's phase shift with input amplitude, caused mainly by voltage-dependent device capacitances; with AM-AM compression it describes a memoryless power amplifier. *First defined in* [21-07](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-07-power-amplifiers.md). *See also:* [Digital predistortion (DPD)](#digital-predistortion-dpd).

<a id="amdahls-law"></a>**Amdahl's law** — Speedup on N processors is 1/((1 − p) + p/N) when a fraction p of the work parallelizes; as N → ∞ it approaches 1/(1 − p), so the serial fraction caps scaling. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="amortized-cost"></a>**Amortized cost** — The average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, in which rare expensive steps are paid for by many cheap ones; a doubling array's append is O(1) amortized. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="amperes-law"></a>**Ampere's law** — (Ampère's law.) For steady currents, ∮ B · dl = µ₀ I_enc around any closed loop; with symmetry it gives the fields of wires, solenoids (µ₀nI), toroids and coaxial cables (zero outside). *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="ampere-hour"></a>**Ampere-hour** — A unit of charge, 1 Ah = 3600 C, used for battery capacity; 1 mAh = 3.6 C. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="amplitude-modulation-am"></a>**Amplitude modulation (AM)** — Carrying a message in a carrier's amplitude, A[1 + m x(t)] cos(2πf_c t); its spectrum is the carrier plus the message's spectrum shifted to ±f_c as two sidebands, occupying twice the message bandwidth. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [DSB-SC modulation](#dsb-sc-modulation), [Modulation index](#modulation-index), [Envelope detector](#envelope-detector).

<a id="amplitude-response"></a>**Amplitude response** — The real function A(ω) in H(e^{jω}) = e^{−jωM/2}A(ω) of a linear-phase FIR filter; it can be negative (the magnitude is |A| and the phase jumps by π), and for symmetric taps it is a sum of cosines. *First defined in* [16-06](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-06-fir-filter-design.md). *See also:* [Linear phase](#linear-phase), [FIR filter](#fir-filter).

<a id="analog-crossbar"></a>**Analog crossbar** — A grid of programmable conductances between row and column wires; with input voltages on the rows and virtual-ground columns, the column currents form the matrix-vector product I = GᵀV. *First defined in* [23-09](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-09-compute-in-memory.md). *See also:* [Differential conductance pair](#differential-conductance-pair), [Compute SNR](#compute-snr).

<a id="analytic-signal"></a>**Analytic signal** — m(t) + j·m̂(t), a complex signal with no negative-frequency content; shifting it to a carrier and taking the real part gives single-sideband modulation. *First defined in* [17-03](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-03-analog-modulation.md). *See also:* [Hilbert transform](#hilbert-transform).

<a id="and-inverter-graph-aig"></a>**And-inverter graph (AIG)** — A logic network of two-input AND nodes with optional inversions on the edges, able to express any function; the internal representation of modern synthesis and verification engines such as ABC. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md). *See also:* [Logic synthesis](#logic-synthesis).

<a id="and-or-invert-aoi-gate"></a>**AND-OR-INVERT (AOI) gate** — A single static CMOS compound gate computing the complement of a sum of products, such as AOI22 = NOT(AB + CD) with 8 transistors; its dual is the OR-AND-INVERT (OAI) gate. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md).

<a id="angle-argument"></a>**Angle (argument)** — The direction ∠z of a complex number's arrow, measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis; computed with the quadrant-aware atan2(y, x). This curriculum reports principal values in (−180°, 180°]. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="angle-condition"></a>**Angle condition** — The requirement that a point s lies on the root locus of 1 + KG(s) = 0 with K > 0, namely that the angle of G(s), the sum of angles from the zeros minus the sum from the poles, is an odd multiple of 180°. *First defined in* [15-06](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-06-root-locus.md). *See also:* [Root locus](#root-locus).

<a id="angle-deficiency"></a>**Angle deficiency** — In root-locus design, the phase a compensator must add at a desired closed-loop pole location so that the loop's total angle there is −180°; a lead compensator's zero and pole are placed to supply it. *First defined in* [15-09](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-09-lead-lag-compensation.md). *See also:* [Angle condition](#angle-condition), [Lead compensator](#lead-compensator).

<a id="angle-random-walk"></a>**Angle random walk** — The growth of orientation error from integrating a gyroscope's white rate noise, as N√(t/2) for a one-sided rate noise density N; quoted in °/√h, equal to 60/√2 times N in °/s/√Hz (the common shortcut 60N assumes a two-sided density). *First defined in* [18-10](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-10-sensors.md). *See also:* [Noise density](#noise-density), [Gyroscope bias](#gyroscope-bias).

<a id="angular-frequency"></a>**Angular frequency** — ω = 2πf, the rate of a sinusoid's phase advance in rad/s, where f is the frequency in hertz. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="anisotropic-etch"></a>**Anisotropic etch** — Etching faster vertically than laterally, achieved in plasmas by directional ion bombardment and sidewall passivation; wet etching is isotropic. *First defined in* [25-03](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-03-deposition-etch-cmp-implant-metrology.md).

<a id="antenna"></a>**Antenna** — A structure that converts guided electromagnetic energy into radiated waves and back; by reciprocity its pattern, gain and impedance are the same for transmitting and receiving. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Radiation pattern](#radiation-pattern), [Antenna gain](#antenna-gain).

<a id="antenna-effect"></a>**Antenna effect** — Damage to thin gate oxide from charge collected by long metal lines during plasma processing, before the line connects to a diffusion. Antenna rules limit the ratio of connected metal area to gate area; fixes are layer jumps and protection diodes. *First defined in* [19-09](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-09-layout-and-standard-cells.md). *See also:* [Design-rule check (DRC)](#design-rule-check-drc).

<a id="antenna-gain"></a>**Antenna gain** — Directivity times radiation efficiency, G = e_r·D, usually quoted in dBi (relative to an isotropic radiator); EIRP = P_t·G_t. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Directivity](#directivity), [Effective aperture](#effective-aperture).

<a id="antenna-noise-temperature"></a>**Antenna noise temperature** — The noise temperature of the power an antenna collects from its surroundings, a pattern-weighted average of the sky and ground brightness temperatures; tens of kelvin for a cold, clear sky, about 290 K for an antenna that sees the ground. *First defined in* [17-02](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-02-noise-and-snr.md). *See also:* [System noise temperature](#system-noise-temperature).

<a id="antenna-tuner"></a>**Antenna tuner** — A network of switched capacitors or inductors that re-matches a phone's antenna (impedance tuning) or moves its resonance (aperture tuning) as hands, heads and bands change it; it pays when the mismatch loss it removes exceeds its own loss. *First defined in* [21-09](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-09-rf-front-end.md). *See also:* [Mismatch loss](#mismatch-loss), [Voltage standing-wave ratio (VSWR)](#voltage-standing-wave-ratio-vswr).

<a id="antenna-in-package-aip"></a>**Antenna-in-package (AiP)** — Integrating millimetre-wave antennas in the same package as the transceiver IC, because package and board routing cost tenths of a dB per millimetre and on-chip antennas are inefficient. *First defined in* [21-10](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-10-antennas-arrays-mmwave.md). *See also:* [Microstrip patch antenna](#microstrip-patch-antenna).

<a id="anti-aliasing-filter"></a>**Anti-aliasing filter** — The analog low-pass (or band-pass) filter before a sampler that attenuates everything that would fold into the band of interest; its requirement is set at the first alias frequency f_s − f_B, and oversampling relaxes it. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Aliasing (sampling)](#aliasing-sampling), [Oversampling](#oversampling).

<a id="anti-imaging-filter"></a>**Anti-imaging filter** — The low-pass filter after an upsampler (or a DAC) that removes the copies of the baseband spectrum at multiples of the original sample rate. *First defined in* [16-09](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-09-multirate-dsp.md). *See also:* [Interpolation (upsampling)](#interpolation-upsampling).

<a id="anti-rollback-counter"></a>**Anti-rollback counter** — A monotonic minimum security version stored in fuses or protected memory; the bootloader refuses images whose security counter is lower, so genuinely signed but vulnerable old images cannot be reinstalled. *First defined in* [18-08](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-08-boot-and-firmware-update.md). *See also:* [Secure boot](#secure-boot), [Rollback](#rollback).

<a id="anti-windup"></a>**Anti-windup** — A modification that stops integrator windup, either by clamping (pausing integration while saturated in the direction that would deepen saturation) or by back-calculation (feeding the difference between the limited and unlimited controller output back into the integrator). *First defined in* [15-08](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-08-pid-control.md). *See also:* [Integrator windup](#integrator-windup).

<a id="antiderivative"></a>**Antiderivative** — A function F with F' = f; any two differ by a constant, written ∫ f dx = F + C. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="antipodal-signalling"></a>**Antipodal signalling** — Binary signalling with s₂ = −s₁ (BPSK, polar NRZ); the largest distance for the energy, 2√Eb, giving Pb = Q(√(2Eb/N0)), 3 dB better than orthogonal or on-off signalling. *First defined in* [17-05](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-05-matched-filters-and-detection.md). *See also:* [Orthogonal signalling](#orthogonal-signalling), [Q-function](#q-function).

<a id="aperture-jitter"></a>**Aperture jitter** — Random variation of a sampler's timing; it turns into noise proportional to the input's slope, limiting SNR to −20 log₁₀(2πf₀σ_t) for a sine at f₀ and RMS jitter σ_t, independent of the sample rate. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Jitter](#jitter).

<a id="apparent-power"></a>**Apparent power** — S = V_rms·I_rms, in volt-amperes; real power is S times the power factor. Wiring and transformers must be sized for S. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md). *See also:* [Power factor](#power-factor).

<a id="application-binary-interface-abi"></a>**Application binary interface (ABI)** — The binary-level contract that lets separately compiled code work together — calling convention, data type sizes and alignment, structure layout and object-file conventions; RISC-V's are ILP32 and LP64 families. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md). *See also:* [Calling convention](#calling-convention).

<a id="application-processor-ap"></a>**Application processor (AP)** — A phone's or tablet's main SoC, integrating CPU clusters, GPU, NPU, image and video processors, display engines, security and often the cellular modem, sharing one memory interface and one thermal budget. *First defined in* [27-02](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-02-smartphone-soc.md). *See also:* [Heterogeneous multicore](#heterogeneous-multicore), [System-level cache (SLC)](#system-level-cache-slc).

<a id="apsk"></a>**APSK** — Amplitude-and-phase-shift keying, points on a few concentric rings; used in satellite links (DVB-S2) because its few amplitude levels suit amplifiers run near saturation. *First defined in* [17-06](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-06-bandpass-digital-modulation.md). *See also:* [QAM](#qam), [M-PSK](#m-psk).

<a id="ar-1-process"></a>**AR(1) process** — The first-order autoregressive sequence x[n] = a x[n-1] + w[n] with white w; its autocorrelation decays as a^|k| and its PSD is σw²/|1 - a e^(-jω)|². Sampling exponentially correlated (RC-filtered) noise produces exactly this sequence. *First defined in* [17-01](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-01-random-processes-and-psd.md). *See also:* [Correlation time](#correlation-time), [Noise folding](#noise-folding).

<a id="arc-length"></a>**Arc length** — The length of a curve, L = ∫√(1 + f'(x)²) dx, built from the element ds = √(dx² + dy²). *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="architecture-license"></a>**Architecture license** — A licence to design one's own processor cores that comply with a licensed ISA, as opposed to using the licensor's core designs; Arm's architecture licensees also pay a per-chip royalty. *First defined in* [14-02](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-02-isa-risc-v-arm-x86.md). *See also:* [Core license](#core-license).

<a id="area-coverage"></a>**Area coverage** — The fraction of a cell's area where the signal exceeds the threshold, higher than the probability at the cell edge because most of the area lies closer in; Jakes's formula relates the two (75 percent at the edge is about 90 percent over the area for σ = 8 dB, n = 3.5). *First defined in* [21-11](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-11-link-budgets.md). *See also:* [Fade margin](#fade-margin).

<a id="area-product"></a>**Area product** — A_p = A_e·W_A, the product of a core's cross-section and winding-window area; an inductor needs A_p ≥ L·I_pk·I_rms/(K_u·J·B_max). *First defined in* [22-05](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-05-magnetics-design.md). *See also:* [Core geometrical constant](#core-geometrical-constant), [Window utilization factor](#window-utilization-factor).

<a id="arithmetic-gradient"></a>**Arithmetic gradient** — A cash-flow series that grows by a fixed amount G each period (0, G, 2G, …); the FE factors (P/G, i, n) = [(1 + i)^n − 1 − ni]/[i²(1 + i)^n] and (A/G, i, n) = 1/i − n/[(1 + i)^n − 1] convert it to a present or uniform annual equivalent. *First defined in* [26-03](../courses/26-engineering-design-and-professional-practice/chapters/26-03-engineering-economics-1.md). *See also:* [Interest factor](#interest-factor).

<a id="arithmetic-intensity"></a>**Arithmetic intensity** — Operations performed per byte moved from memory. A workload whose intensity is below a machine's ridge point (peak operations per second ÷ memory bandwidth) is memory-bound; a matrix–vector product has about 1 flop per byte in 16-bit precision. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="arithmetic-logic-unit-alu"></a>**Arithmetic-logic unit (ALU)** — A block that performs one of several arithmetic and logical operations on two words, chosen by an operation code, and reports status flags; the computational core of a processor datapath. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md). *See also:* [Status flags](#status-flags).

<a id="arp"></a>**ARP** — The Address Resolution Protocol, which finds the MAC address of a neighbour with a given IPv4 address by broadcasting a request and caching the reply. *First defined in* [17-13](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-13-computer-networks-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [MAC address](#mac-address).

<a id="array-efficiency"></a>**Array efficiency** — The fraction of a memory macro's area occupied by bitcells: macro density divided by the bitcells' raw density; about 80% for the densest 2025 SRAM macros and lower for fast ones. *First defined in* [23-02](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-02-sram-technology.md). *See also:* [SRAM macro](#sram-macro).

<a id="array-factor"></a>**Array factor** — The pattern of an array of identical isotropic elements, set by their spacing and relative phases; the array's pattern is the element pattern times the array factor, and a progressive phase steers the beam. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Phased array](#phased-array).

<a id="array-gain"></a>**Array gain** — The SNR increase from coherently combining N antennas against independent noise, a factor N (10 log10 N dB); it shifts error-rate curves without changing their slope. *First defined in* [17-11](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-11-mimo-and-beamforming.md). *See also:* [Diversity order](#diversity-order), [Maximal-ratio combining](#maximal-ratio-combining), [Spatial multiplexing](#spatial-multiplexing).

<a id="arrhenius-model"></a>**Arrhenius model** — A thermally activated rate ∝ exp(−E_a/(kT)); the acceleration factor between temperatures is exp[(E_a/k)(1/T_use − 1/T_stress)], exponential in the often-uncertain activation energy. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="asil"></a>**ASIL** — Automotive Safety Integrity Level, from A (least demanding) to D (most demanding), assigned to a safety goal from the severity, exposure and controllability of the hazard it prevents; QM marks hazards needing only normal quality management. *First defined in* [25-10](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-10-qualification-and-functional-safety.md). *See also:* [ISO 26262](#iso-26262), [Safety goal](#safety-goal).

<a id="assembler"></a>**Assembler** — The tool that translates assembly language, instruction by instruction, into machine code in an object file, leaving addresses it cannot know as relocations for the linker. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md). *See also:* [Object file](#object-file), [Linker](#linker).

<a id="assertion"></a>**Assertion** — A statement (assert condition) that stops the program if a condition the code relies on is false; used for internal invariants and tests, not for validating input, because python -O removes assertions. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md).

<a id="assumed-state-method"></a>**Assumed-state method** — Analyzing a circuit with diodes by guessing which conduct, replacing each with its on or off model, solving the linear circuit, and checking every guess for consistency. *First defined in* [10-01](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-01-diodes-and-diode-circuits.md).

<a id="asymptote"></a>**Asymptote** — A line that a curve approaches in a limit, horizontal (x → ∞), vertical (f → ±∞ at a finite x) or slanted; Bode-plot straight lines are asymptotes of a frequency response. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="asymptote-centroid"></a>**Asymptote centroid** — The point (Σ poles − Σ zeros)/(n − m) on the real axis from which the n − m asymptotes of a root locus radiate, at angles (2k + 1)·180°/(n − m). *First defined in* [15-06](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-06-root-locus.md). *See also:* [Root locus](#root-locus).

<a id="asymptotic-gain-formula"></a>**Asymptotic-gain formula** — The exact closed-loop gain of a circuit with one controlled source, A_f = A∞·T/(1 + T) + A0/(1 + T), where A∞ is the gain with the controlling variable forced to zero, A0 the gain with the source set to zero, and T the return ratio. *First defined in* [12-05](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-05-feedback-topologies.md). *See also:* [Return ratio](#return-ratio).

<a id="asynchronous-fifo"></a>**Asynchronous FIFO** — A dual-port memory written in one clock domain and read in another, whose Gray-coded read and write pointers cross the domains through synchronizers and produce conservative full and empty flags. *First defined in* [08-10](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-10-timing-metastability-cdc.md). *See also:* [Clock-domain crossing (CDC)](#clock-domain-crossing-cdc).

<a id="asynchronous-reset"></a>**Asynchronous reset** — A reset that acts on a flip-flop immediately, without a clock; its release must meet a recovery time before the next clock edge, so it is usually asserted asynchronously and released through a reset synchronizer. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md). *See also:* [Recovery time](#recovery-time).

<a id="atomic-layer-deposition-ald"></a>**Atomic-layer deposition (ALD)** — Deposition in alternating self-limiting half-reactions separated by purges, adding a fixed fraction of a nanometre per cycle; conformal and precisely controlled, but slow. *First defined in* [25-03](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-03-deposition-etch-cmp-implant-metrology.md).

<a id="atomic-layer-etching-ale"></a>**Atomic-layer etching (ALE)** — Etching in self-limiting cycles of surface modification and removal, taking off a fixed thin layer per cycle with high uniformity and selectivity. *First defined in* [25-03](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-03-deposition-etch-cmp-implant-metrology.md).

<a id="auger-recombination"></a>**Auger recombination** — Recombination in which the released energy goes to a third carrier, at rate (C_n n + C_p p)(np − n_i²); it dominates at high doping, limiting the lifetime of heavily doped regions and the efficiency of silicon solar cells. *First defined in* [09-04](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-04-generation-recombination-continuity.md).

<a id="auracast"></a>**Auracast** — The marketing name for Bluetooth LE Audio broadcast, in which one transmitter sends isochronous audio streams that any number of receivers can join without acknowledgment. *First defined in* [27-04](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-04-wearables-earbuds-and-glasses.md). *See also:* [LE Audio](#le-audio).

<a id="autocorrelation-function"></a>**Autocorrelation function** — R_X(t₁, t₂) = E[X(t₁)X(t₂)]; for a stationary process R_X(τ), whose value at τ = 0 is the average power and whose decay measures how long the process remembers. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="automatic-test-equipment-ate"></a>**Automatic test equipment (ATE)** — A production tester with hundreds to thousands of precisely timed channels that drive and compare a chip's pins and measure its parametrics; the market is dominated by Advantest and Teradyne. *First defined in* [25-11](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-11-test-ate-sort-burn-in.md). *See also:* [Wafer sort](#wafer-sort), [Final test](#final-test).

<a id="automatic-test-pattern-generation-atpg"></a>**Automatic test pattern generation (ATPG)** — Algorithms (D-algorithm, PODEM, FAN and successors) that find input patterns detecting each target fault by activating it, propagating the difference to an observable point and justifying the required values. *First defined in* [19-12](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-12-design-for-test.md). *See also:* [Stuck-at fault](#stuck-at-fault), [Fault coverage](#fault-coverage).

<a id="automotive-ethernet"></a>**Automotive Ethernet** — Ethernet variants for vehicles that run over single twisted pairs, from the 10BASE-T1S multidrop bus to 100 Mb/s, 1 Gb/s and multi-gigabit point-to-point links used for backbones and high-rate sensors. *First defined in* [27-06](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-06-automotive-ee-architecture.md). *See also:* [Zone controller](#zone-controller).

<a id="auxiliary-polynomial"></a>**Auxiliary polynomial** — In a Routh array with a row of zeros, the even or odd polynomial formed from the row above; it divides the original polynomial, and its roots (symmetric about the origin, often an imaginary-axis pair) give the oscillation frequency at a stability boundary. *First defined in* [15-05](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-05-stability-routh-hurwitz.md). *See also:* [Routh array](#routh-array).

<a id="available-noise-power"></a>**Available noise power** — The largest noise power a source can deliver, which it delivers to a matched load: kT·B for a resistor at temperature T in bandwidth B, independent of the resistance; −174 dBm/Hz at 290 K. *First defined in* [17-02](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-02-noise-and-snr.md). *See also:* [Thermal noise](#thermal-noise), [Noise temperature](#noise-temperature).

<a id="avalanche-breakdown"></a>**Avalanche breakdown** — Reverse breakdown in which the ionization integral reaches 1 and multiplication becomes self-sustaining; it dominates in silicon above a few volts, its voltage falls roughly as N^(−0.6) to N^(−0.75) and rises with temperature. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md). *See also:* [Critical field](#critical-field), [Tunneling breakdown](#tunneling-breakdown).

<a id="avalanche-multiplication"></a>**Avalanche multiplication** — The growth of a reverse current by repeated impact ionization in a depletion region, measured by the multiplication factor M, where 1 − 1/M equals the ionization integral; M diverges at breakdown. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="avalanche-photodiode"></a>**Avalanche photodiode** — A photodiode biased near breakdown so that photogenerated carriers are multiplied by impact ionization (APD), giving gain at the cost of extra noise. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="average-real-power"></a>**Average (real) power** — P = (V_m I_m/2) cos θ = V_rms I_rms cos θ (watts), the time average of p = vi for sinusoids; only resistance absorbs it, and it is the real part of complex power. *First defined in* [07-06](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-06-ac-power-and-power-factor.md).

<a id="average-active-efficiency"></a>**Average active efficiency** — The regulatory efficiency metric for external power supplies in the EU and US, the mean of the efficiencies at 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of rated output, paired with a separate no-load power limit. *First defined in* [22-01](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-01-power-conversion-principles.md). *See also:* [Efficiency](#efficiency).

<a id="average-memory-access-time-amat"></a>**Average memory access time (AMAT)** — Hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty, nested for each level of the hierarchy; the average latency a memory access sees. *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md). *See also:* [Miss rate](#miss-rate).

<a id="average-pixel-level-apl"></a>**Average pixel level (APL)** — The average over all pixels of each pixel's luminance as a fraction of full-white luminance; an emissive (OLED) display's emission power is proportional to it, which is why always-on watch faces are mostly black. *First defined in* [27-03](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-03-wearables-smartwatch.md). *See also:* [Always-on display (AOD)](#always-on-display-aod), [Luminance](#luminance).

<a id="average-power"></a>**Average power** — The energy delivered over an interval divided by its length, (1/T)∫p dt; for varying signals it is the average of v·i, not the product of the averages. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="average-power-tracking-apt"></a>**Average power tracking (APT)** — Adjusting a power amplifier's supply slowly, once per time slot, to suit the average transmit power, which recovers efficiency at low power without a wideband modulator. *First defined in* [21-07](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-07-power-amplifiers.md). *See also:* [Envelope tracking (ET)](#envelope-tracking-et).

<a id="average-value"></a>**Average value** — (1/(b − a)) ∫_a^b f dx, the height of the rectangle with the same area; over one period it is a signal's DC value. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="averaged-model"></a>**Averaged model** — A converter model obtained by averaging its state equations over one switching period, replacing the switch by controlled sources such as d·v_g; valid for signals well below the switching frequency. *First defined in* [22-07](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-07-converter-dynamics-and-control.md). *See also:* [Small-ripple approximation](#small-ripple-approximation).

<a id="avsbus"></a>**AVSBus** — A PMBus point-to-point, SPI-like interface at up to 50 MHz through which a processor or FPGA sets its own supply voltage on a voltage regulator, used for adaptive and dynamic voltage scaling in servers. *First defined in* [22-08](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-08-pmics.md). *See also:* [Adaptive voltage scaling (AVS)](#adaptive-voltage-scaling-avs).

<a id="awgn-channel"></a>**AWGN channel** — The additive white Gaussian noise model r(t) = s(t) + n(t), with n zero-mean, white with two-sided density N0/2, Gaussian and independent of the signal; the benchmark on which modulations and codes are compared. *First defined in* [17-02](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-02-noise-and-snr.md). *See also:* [White noise](#white-noise), [Eb/N0](#eb-n0).

<a id="axi"></a>**AXI** — Arm's AMBA Advanced eXtensible Interface, a royalty-free on-chip bus protocol with five independent valid/ready channels (write address, write data, write response, read address, read data), bursts and multiple outstanding transactions; AXI-Lite is its simple register-access subset. *First defined in* [14-11](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-11-io-buses-and-interconnect.md). *See also:* [Valid/ready handshake](#valid-ready-handshake).

<a id="axial-ratio"></a>**Axial ratio** — The ratio of the major to the minor axis of the ellipse traced by a wave's electric field; 1 for circular polarization and infinite for linear. A linear antenna on an axial-ratio-r wave captures between 1/(1 + r²) and r²/(1 + r²) of the power. *First defined in* [13-05](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-05-plane-waves.md). *See also:* [Polarization (light)](#polarization-light).

<a id="letter-b"></a>

## B

<a id="b10-life"></a>**B10 life** — The time by which 10% of a population has failed, α(−ln 0.9)^(1/γ) for a Weibull; percentile lives matter more than MTTF for wear-out. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="back-end-of-line-beol"></a>**Back end of line (BEOL)** — The stack of metal wiring layers and vias built above the transistors, typically copper in low-k dielectric, tiered from tight local layers to thick global ones and processed at about 400 °C or below. *First defined in* [25-01](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-01-process-flow-overview.md). *See also:* [Dual damascene](#dual-damascene), [Middle of line (MOL)](#middle-of-line-mol).

<a id="back-drilling"></a>**Back-drilling** — Drilling out the unused stub of a plated via from the far side of the board, so its quarter-wave notch moves far above the Nyquist frequency. *First defined in* [24-01](../courses/24-high-speed-io-signal-integrity-and-photonics/chapters/24-01-signal-integrity-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [Via stub](#via-stub).

<a id="back-emf"></a>**Back-EMF** — The EMF a running motor's rotating coil generates against its supply, proportional to speed; it limits running current, so a stalled motor draws far more current than a spinning one. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="back-gate-biasing"></a>**Back-gate biasing** — Shifting an FD-SOI transistor's threshold by biasing the substrate region under the buried oxide; the coupling C_Si·C_BOX/[C_ox(C_Si + C_BOX)] is tens of millivolts per volt and rises as the BOX thins. *First defined in* [25-05](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-05-foundries-pdks-specialty-processes.md).

<a id="background-calibration"></a>**Background calibration** — Calibration that estimates and corrects a circuit's errors continuously while it operates, so that it tracks temperature and supply drift without interrupting the signal. *First defined in* [20-12](../courses/20-analog-and-mixed-signal-ic-design/chapters/20-12-why-analog-does-not-scale.md). *See also:* [Digitally assisted analog](#digitally-assisted-analog).

<a id="backside-power-delivery"></a>**Backside power delivery** — Routing a chip's power supply through thick wires on the back of the thinned wafer, freeing front-side wiring for signals and cutting IR drop; Intel ships it as PowerVia on 18A, and TSMC plans it for A16. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="baligas-figure-of-merit"></a>**Baliga's figure of merit** — The material figure εμE_c³ that sets the lowest specific on-resistance of a unipolar power device at a given blocking voltage; the cube on the critical field gives wide-bandgap materials their advantage. *First defined in* [09-13](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-13-compound-and-wide-bandgap-semiconductors.md). *See also:* [Specific on-resistance](#specific-on-resistance), [Critical field](#critical-field).

<a id="ballistic-transport"></a>**Ballistic transport** — Carrier motion across a region shorter than a few mean free paths, with few or no collisions, where mobility and velocity saturation lose their meaning; modern short-channel transistors are partly ballistic. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md).

<a id="balloting-group"></a>**Balloting group** — The members eligible to vote on a draft standard; under IEEE SA rules at least 75% must return ballots and at least 75% of Approve plus Do Not Approve votes must approve, and 30% or more abstentions invalidate the ballot. *First defined in* [26-02](../courses/26-engineering-design-and-professional-practice/chapters/26-02-design-reviews-and-standards.md).

<a id="band-gap"></a>**Band gap** — The range of energies with no allowed electron states between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band, E_g = E_c − E_v (1.12 eV in silicon); it sets intrinsic carrier density, absorption edge and breakdown strength. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="band-gap-narrowing"></a>**Band-gap narrowing** — The reduction of a semiconductor's band gap at high doping, tens of meV near 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ in silicon, which raises the effective n_i² of the region exponentially and affects bipolar emitters and solar cells. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md).

<a id="band-pass-sampling"></a>**Band-pass sampling** — Sampling a band f_L–f_H below twice its highest frequency by placing it inside one Nyquist zone: 2f_H/n ≤ f_s ≤ 2f_L/(n − 1); the band reappears between 0 and f_s/2, inverted when n is even. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Nyquist zone](#nyquist-zone), [Aliasing (sampling)](#aliasing-sampling).

<a id="bandgap-reference"></a>**Bandgap reference** — A circuit that adds a junction voltage (falling about 2 mV/K) to a voltage proportional to absolute temperature so that the temperature coefficients cancel; its output sits near the silicon bandgap, about 1.2 V. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="bandwidth"></a>**Bandwidth** — The frequency extent of a spectrum or a frequency response; it must be defined (−3 dB, null-to-null, fractional-energy such as 99%, or Nyquist frequency of a symbol stream), since the definitions can differ by large factors for one signal. *First defined in* [11-06](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-06-continuous-time-fourier-transform.md).

<a id="bandwidth-separation"></a>**Bandwidth separation** — Designing nested (cascade) loops so each outer loop is several times (typically 5 to 10) slower than the loop inside it, which lets the outer loop treat the inner one as an ideal actuator. *First defined in* [15-12](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-12-control-applications-pll-regulators-thermal.md).

<a id="bandwidth-delay-product"></a>**Bandwidth-delay product** — The data in flight needed to keep a path busy, rate × round-trip time (5 MB for 1 Gb/s over 40 ms); a TCP window smaller than this limits throughput to window/RTT. *First defined in* [17-13](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-13-computer-networks-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [TCP](#tcp), [Congestion window](#congestion-window).

<a id="bang-bang-phase-detector"></a>**Bang-bang phase detector** — A clock-recovery phase detector that outputs only early or late from data and edge samples; random jitter of rms σ linearizes it to a gain of about √(2/π)/σ, so the loop's bandwidth depends on the incoming jitter, and it saturates for errors of a few σ. *First defined in* [24-03](../courses/24-high-speed-io-signal-integrity-and-photonics/chapters/24-03-serdes-architecture.md). *See also:* [Clock and data recovery (CDR)](#clock-and-data-recovery-cdr).

<a id="bank-conflict"></a>**Bank conflict** — Several lanes of a warp accessing different words in the same shared-memory bank, which serializes the access; for a word stride s with 32 banks, the conflict degree is gcd(s, 32). *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [Shared memory (GPU)](#shared-memory-gpu).

<a id="bank-group"></a>**Bank group** — A set of DRAM banks that share column circuitry; consecutive column commands to different groups can issue every tCCD_S, to the same group only every longer tCCD_L, so the pin rate can rise without speeding up every core. *First defined in* [23-04](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-04-dram-interfaces.md). *See also:* [DRAM bank](#dram-bank), [Burst length](#burst-length).

<a id="barkhausen-criterion"></a>**Barkhausen criterion** — The condition for a sustained oscillation in a positive-feedback loop, loop gain exactly 1 with zero phase at the oscillation frequency; practical oscillators start with loop gain above 1 and rely on a nonlinearity to bring it to 1. *First defined in* [12-09](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-09-oscillators.md). *See also:* [Describing function](#describing-function), [Loop gain](#loop-gain).

<a id="barrel-shifter"></a>**Barrel shifter** — A shifter that shifts by any amount in one pass, built from log2 n stages of 2-to-1 multiplexers, stage k shifting by 2^k. *First defined in* [08-09](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md).

<a id="base-die"></a>**Base die** — The bottom die of an HBM stack, holding the PHY, test, repair and power-distribution logic; from HBM4 it moves to a logic process, which allows customer-specific functions. *First defined in* [23-05](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-05-hbm-in-depth.md). *See also:* [Custom HBM](#custom-hbm).

<a id="base-transport-factor"></a>**Base transport factor** — The fraction α_T of carriers injected into the base that reach the collector without recombining, 1 − W_B²/2L_B²; essentially 1 in modern thin-base transistors. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="base-rate-effect"></a>**Base-rate effect** — Even an accurate test produces mostly false positives when the condition it detects is rare, because its false-positive rate applies to the large unaffected majority. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="baseband-processor-modem"></a>**Baseband processor (modem)** — The digital engine between a radio's converters and the network stack, running filtering, FFTs, channel estimation, MIMO detection, demapping, HARQ, channel decoding and the protocol layers; its silicon cost is dominated by the datapath, the decoders and the buffers. *First defined in* [21-12](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-12-modem-baseband-and-standards.md). *See also:* [Hybrid ARQ (HARQ)](#hybrid-arq-harq), [Soft buffer](#soft-buffer).

<a id="baseline"></a>**Baseline** — A reviewed and approved version of a document or design that changes only through a controlled process (change requests approved by a change control board); specification freeze establishes the baseline that design and verification work to. *First defined in* [26-02](../courses/26-engineering-design-and-professional-practice/chapters/26-02-design-reviews-and-standards.md). *See also:* [Change control board](#change-control-board), [Specification freeze](#specification-freeze).

<a id="baseline-wander"></a>**Baseline wander** — The drift of a received signal's average level when a long run of one symbol passes through an AC-coupled channel that cannot carry DC; DC-balanced line codes prevent it. *First defined in* [17-04](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-04-baseband-digital-transmission.md). *See also:* [Line code](#line-code).

<a id="basepri"></a>**BASEPRI** — A Cortex-M special register that masks every exception whose priority value is greater than or equal to its own, letting more urgent interrupts through; the basis of critical sections that keep the tightest deadlines live. *First defined in* [18-03](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-03-interrupts-exceptions-timers.md). *See also:* [Interrupt priority](#interrupt-priority).

<a id="basis"></a>**Basis** — A set of independent vectors that spans a subspace; every vector in the subspace is then a unique combination of the basis vectors. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="bathtub-curve"></a>**Bathtub curve** — A curve shaped like a bathtub, used in two senses: bit error rate against sampling instant across the unit interval, and failure rate against age (infant mortality, flat mid-life, wear-out). *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="battery-protection-circuit"></a>**Battery protection circuit** — An IC and back-to-back MOSFETs in a lithium-ion pack that disconnect the cell on overvoltage, undervoltage, overcurrent or short circuit, independently of the charger and gauge. *First defined in* [22-09](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-09-batteries-charging-fuel-gauging.md).

<a id="baud-rate"></a>**Baud rate** — Symbols per second on a serial line; for a UART, bits per second including start, stop and parity bits, generated by dividing a clock (with integer or fractional divisors whose error must fit the receiver's tolerance). *First defined in* [18-05](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-05-gpio-uart-spi-i2c.md). *See also:* [UART](#uart).

<a id="bayes-rule"></a>**Bayes' rule** — P(A | B) = P(A) P(B | A)/P(B), which turns the probability of an observation given a cause into the probability of the cause given the observation. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md). *See also:* [Base-rate effect](#base-rate-effect), [Maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection](#maximum-a-posteriori-map-detection).

<a id="bcd-process"></a>**BCD process** — A bipolar-CMOS-DMOS process combining logic, precision analog and high-voltage LDMOS transistors on one die, used for power management, motor drivers and battery management. *First defined in* [25-05](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-05-foundries-pdks-specialty-processes.md).

<a id="bch-code"></a>**BCH code** — A binary cyclic code of length 2^m − 1 whose generator polynomial has 2t consecutive powers of a primitive element as roots, guaranteeing d_min ≥ 2t + 1 with at most mt check bits; Reed–Solomon codes are the non-binary case. *First defined in* [17-08](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-08-channel-coding.md). *See also:* [Reed–Solomon code](#reed-solomon-code).

<a id="beachfront-die-edge"></a>**Beachfront (die edge)** — The length of a die's perimeter available for off-die signal bumps; because it grows only as the square root of die area, it limits how many interface pins, and so how much off-chip bandwidth, a die can have. *First defined in* [23-01](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-01-memory-hierarchy-and-memory-wall.md).

<a id="beam-squint"></a>**Beam squint** — The drift of a phase-shifter array's beam with frequency, sin θ = (f₀/f) sin θ₀, because a fixed phase equals the needed delay only at the design frequency; it limits the bandwidth of large, widely scanned arrays. *First defined in* [21-10](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-10-antennas-arrays-mmwave.md). *See also:* [True-time delay](#true-time-delay).

<a id="beats"></a>**Beats** — The slow swelling and fading of a sum of two sinusoids of nearly equal frequency, or of an undamped system forced near its natural frequency; the envelope varies at half the difference frequency. *First defined in* [02-04](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-04-forced-response-and-resonance.md).

<a id="belief-propagation"></a>**Belief propagation** — Iterative decoding in which variable nodes add incoming log-likelihood ratios and check nodes combine them with the tanh rule (or its min-sum approximation), refining every bit's belief each iteration. *First defined in* [17-08](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-08-channel-coding.md). *See also:* [LDPC code](#ldpc-code), [Log-likelihood ratio (LLR)](#log-likelihood-ratio-llr).

<a id="bellman-ford-algorithm"></a>**Bellman–Ford algorithm** — The iterative shortest-path update d_x(y) = min_v [c(x, v) + d_v(y)] used by distance-vector routing; it handles negative costs but can count to infinity after failures. *First defined in* [17-13](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-13-computer-networks-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [Dijkstra's algorithm](#dijkstras-algorithm).

<a id="benchmark"></a>**Benchmark** — A fixed workload with rules for how it is run and reported, used to compare systems; its rules (fixed code, accuracy targets, mandatory baselines) are what make results comparable. *First defined in* [14-15](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-15-roofline-and-benchmarks.md). *See also:* [SPEC CPU](#spec-cpu), [MLPerf](#mlperf).

<a id="benefit-cost-ratio"></a>**Benefit–cost ratio** — The present value of benefits divided by the present value of costs; a project passes if it exceeds 1 (equivalent to NPV > 0), and mutually exclusive alternatives are compared on the incremental ratio ΔB/ΔC, not on their own ratios. *First defined in* [26-03](../courses/26-engineering-design-and-professional-practice/chapters/26-03-engineering-economics-1.md). *See also:* [Net present value (NPV)](#net-present-value-npv).

<a id="bernoulli-equation"></a>**Bernoulli equation** — y' + p(t)y = q(t)yⁿ, made linear by the substitution v = y^(1−n); the logistic equation is the case n = 2. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="bessel-filter"></a>**Bessel filter** — A filter whose poles are chosen for maximally flat group delay, preserving pulse shapes with almost no overshoot, at the cost of a gentle magnitude roll-off. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [Group delay](#group-delay), [Elliptic filter](#elliptic-filter).

<a id="beta-helper"></a>**Beta helper** — A transistor added to a bipolar current mirror to supply the mirror's base currents from the supply, cutting the reference's base-current loss by a factor of about β. *First defined in* [10-08](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-08-current-sources-and-mirrors.md).

<a id="beta-multiplier"></a>**Beta multiplier** — A self-biased MOS current reference in which two transistors of width ratio M, one with a source resistor R, are forced to equal currents by a mirror; in weak inversion with grounded bulks it gives I = V_T ln M/R, a PTAT current, and it needs a startup circuit. *First defined in* [20-03](../courses/20-analog-and-mixed-signal-ic-design/chapters/20-03-bandgap-references.md). *See also:* [Startup circuit](#startup-circuit), [PTAT voltage](#ptat-voltage), [Weak inversion](#weak-inversion).

<a id="beta-factor-model"></a>**Beta-factor model** — A model of common-cause failure in which a fraction β of each channel's failures is shared, so two channels both fail with probability about βp + [(1 − β)p]² rather than p². *First defined in* [26-07](../courses/26-engineering-design-and-professional-practice/chapters/26-07-engineering-ethics.md).

<a id="bfloat16"></a>**bfloat16** — A 16-bit floating-point format with 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 fraction bits; it keeps FP32's range (about 3.4×10^38) at about 2.4 decimal digits of precision, and FP32 converts to it by rounding away the low 16 bits. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md). *See also:* [Floating-point number](#floating-point-number), [FP8](#fp8).

<a id="bias"></a>**Bias** — The difference between an estimator's expected value and the true parameter; mean square error equals bias squared plus variance. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="bias-temperature-instability-bti"></a>**Bias-temperature instability (BTI)** — A gradual, partly recoverable shift in transistor threshold voltage under gate bias at elevated temperature (NBTI for PMOS, PBTI for NMOS), growing roughly as a power of stress time with a disputed exponent. *First defined in* [25-09](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-09-reliability-physics.md). *See also:* [Hot-carrier injection (HCI)](#hot-carrier-injection-hci).

<a id="bibo-stability"></a>**BIBO stability** — Bounded-input, bounded-output stability; every bounded input produces a bounded output. An LTI system is BIBO-stable exactly when its impulse response is absolutely summable (integrable); accumulators, integrators and lossless resonators are not. *First defined in* [11-02](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-02-system-properties.md). *See also:* [Stability (of a circuit)](#stability-of-a-circuit).

<a id="bicmos"></a>**BiCMOS** — A process that integrates bipolar (often SiGe heterojunction) transistors with CMOS on one chip, for RF, mmWave and precision analog functions alongside digital logic, at the cost of extra process steps. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="big-o-notation"></a>**Big-O notation** — f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g for large n; it keeps an algorithm's growth rate (constant, log n, n, n log n, n squared) and drops constant factors. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="bilateral-laplace-transform"></a>**Bilateral Laplace transform** — X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^{−st} dt over all t, with s = σ + jω: the Fourier transform of x(t)e^{−σt}; it describes signals and systems for all time and is meaningful only together with its region of convergence. *First defined in* [11-08](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-08-laplace-transform-and-system-functions.md). *See also:* [Laplace transform](#laplace-transform), [Region of convergence (ROC)](#region-of-convergence-roc).

<a id="bilinear-transform"></a>**Bilinear transform** — The s-to-z map s = (2/T)(1 − z^{−1})/(1 + z^{−1}), from the trapezoidal rule: it maps the left half-plane into the unit disk and the whole jω axis onto the unit circle once, so stability is kept and there is no aliasing, at the cost of frequency warping. *First defined in* [11-09](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-09-z-transform.md). *See also:* [Frequency warping](#frequency-warping), [Impulse invariance](#impulse-invariance).

<a id="bill-of-materials-bom"></a>**Bill of materials (BOM)** — The list of a product's components and their costs; the BOM plus assembly, test, royalties and logistics gives the cost of goods sold, and a change in any component's cost moves gross margin by that change divided by the selling price. *First defined in* [27-01](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-01-system-analysis-method.md). *See also:* [Budget tree](#budget-tree).

<a id="binary-decision-diagram-bdd"></a>**Binary decision diagram (BDD)** — A graph representation of a Boolean function as a decision diagram; reduced and ordered (ROBDD), it is canonical for a fixed variable order, so equivalence is a graph comparison, but its size depends strongly on the order. *First defined in* [19-13](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-13-verification-methods.md). *See also:* [Logic equivalence checking (LEC)](#logic-equivalence-checking-lec), [Model checking](#model-checking).

<a id="binary-entropy-function"></a>**Binary entropy function** — The entropy of a binary source with probabilities p and 1 − p: h(p) = −p log2 p − (1 − p) log2(1 − p); 1 bit at p = 0.5, 0.469 bits at p = 0.1. *First defined in* [17-07](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-07-information-theory-and-shannon.md). *See also:* [Entropy (information)](#entropy-information), [Binary symmetric channel](#binary-symmetric-channel).

<a id="binary-erasure-channel"></a>**Binary erasure channel** — A channel that loses each bit with probability ε but marks the loss; its capacity is 1 − ε, much more than a binary symmetric channel with the same error probability. *First defined in* [17-07](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-07-information-theory-and-shannon.md). *See also:* [Binary symmetric channel](#binary-symmetric-channel).

<a id="binary-heap"></a>**Binary heap** — A complete binary tree stored in an array (children of i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2) with every parent no larger than its children; supports a priority queue with O(log n) insertion and removal of the minimum. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="binary-search"></a>**Binary search** — Searching a sorted array by comparing with the middle element and discarding half each step; at most floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons (20 for a million items). *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="binary-search-tree"></a>**Binary search tree** — A tree whose nodes keep smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right, so search, insertion and deletion cost O(height); self-balancing variants (red-black, AVL, B-trees) keep the height O(log n). *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="binary-symmetric-channel"></a>**Binary symmetric channel** — A channel that flips each bit independently with probability p; its capacity is 1 − h(p) bits per use (0.919 at p = 0.01). *First defined in* [17-07](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-07-information-theory-and-shannon.md). *See also:* [Binary entropy function](#binary-entropy-function), [Binary erasure channel](#binary-erasure-channel).

<a id="binary-coded-decimal-bcd"></a>**Binary-coded decimal (BCD)** — Storing each decimal digit in its own 4-bit group (97 is 1001 0111); it wastes 6 of 16 patterns per digit, and binary addition of BCD digits needs a +6 correction when a digit sum exceeds 9. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md).
