<a id="state-assignment"></a>**State assignment** — The choice of binary code for each state of an FSM (binary, Gray-ordered, one-hot, output-encoded), which sets the number of flip-flops and strongly affects the size and speed of the next-state logic. *First defined in* [08-08](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-08-finite-state-machines.md). *See also:* [One-hot encoding](#one-hot-encoding).

<a id="state-diagram"></a>**State diagram** — A drawing of an FSM with states as circles and transitions as arrows labeled with the input condition (and, for a Mealy machine, the output). *First defined in* [08-08](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-08-finite-state-machines.md). *See also:* [State table](#state-table).

<a id="state-equations"></a>**State equations** — A circuit's first-order differential equations written for its state variables (capacitor voltages and inductor currents), ẋ = Ax + g·u; the eigenvalues of the state matrix A are the circuit's natural frequencies. *First defined in* [07-03](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-03-second-order-rlc-transients.md). *See also:* [State variable](#state-variable).

<a id="state-observer"></a>**State observer** — A model of the plant run in parallel with it and corrected by the output error, x̂' = A x̂ + B u + L(y − C x̂); its estimation error decays with the eigenvalues of A − LC, which L places when (A, C) is observable. Also called a Luenberger observer. *First defined in* [15-10](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-10-state-space-introduction.md). *See also:* [Observability](#observability), [Separation principle](#separation-principle).

<a id="state-of-charge-soc"></a>**State of charge (SOC)** — The fraction of a cell's usable charge still stored, from 0 (empty) to 1 (full); its open-circuit voltage is a function of it, and fuel gauges estimate it. *First defined in* [22-09](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-09-batteries-charging-fuel-gauging.md). *See also:* [Open-circuit voltage](#open-circuit-voltage), [Fuel gauge](#fuel-gauge).

<a id="state-of-health-soh"></a>**State of health (SOH)** — A cell's present capacity (and sometimes resistance) relative to its new value, used to report aging and to adjust gauging and peak-power limits. *First defined in* [22-09](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-09-batteries-charging-fuel-gauging.md).

<a id="state-residency"></a>**State residency** — The fraction of time a processor or package spends in each power state; average power is the residency-weighted sum of the states' powers, so long residency in deep idle dominates light-load battery life. *First defined in* [27-05](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-05-pc-soc.md). *See also:* [Package C-state](#package-c-state).

<a id="state-table"></a>**State table** — A table listing, for each present state and input value, the next state and the output of an FSM; the starting point for deriving its logic. *First defined in* [08-08](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-08-finite-state-machines.md). *See also:* [State diagram](#state-diagram), [State assignment](#state-assignment).

<a id="state-variable"></a>**State variable** — A variable that fully captures a circuit's stored energy and memory, namely capacitor voltages and inductor currents. Knowing them at one instant (plus the inputs) determines the future response. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="state-space-model"></a>**State-space model** — The description x' = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du of a linear system, with state vector x (for circuits, capacitor voltages and inductor currents); the eigenvalues of A are the system's poles. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md). *See also:* [State variable](#state-variable), [Matrix exponential](#matrix-exponential), [Transfer function](#transfer-function).

<a id="static-cmos"></a>**Static CMOS** — The standard logic style in which each gate has a pMOS pull-up network and a dual nMOS pull-down network, exactly one conducting for every input, so the output is always driven to a rail and no current flows once it settles. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md). *See also:* [Pull-up and pull-down networks](#pull-up-and-pull-down-networks).

<a id="static-discipline"></a>**Static discipline** — The rule defining valid digital levels with separate output (V_OL, V_OH) and input (V_IL, V_IH) thresholds, so that every gate restores clean levels and leaves noise margins. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md). *See also:* [Noise margin](#noise-margin).

<a id="static-error-constants"></a>**Static error constants** — K_p = lim L(s), K_v = lim sL(s) and K_a = lim s²L(s) as s → 0; a stable unity-feedback loop's steady errors to a unit step, ramp and parabola are 1/(1 + K_p), 1/K_v and 1/K_a. *First defined in* [15-04](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-04-feedback-and-steady-state-error.md). *See also:* [System type](#system-type), [Steady-state error](#steady-state-error).

<a id="static-noise-margin"></a>**Static noise margin** — For a bistable cell such as an SRAM, the side of the largest square that fits inside the smaller lobe of its butterfly plot (one inverter's transfer curve with the other's mirrored): the largest static offset the cell tolerates. The read SNM is smaller than the hold SNM. *First defined in* [19-08](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-08-sram-design.md). *See also:* [Noise margin](#noise-margin), [SRAM](#sram).

<a id="static-power"></a>**Static power** — The power a circuit draws when it is not switching, V_DD times the total leakage current; it dominates idle and standby energy. *First defined in* [09-11](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-11-cmos-and-scaling.md).

<a id="static-timing-analysis-sta"></a>**Static timing analysis (STA)** — Checking every timing path of a synchronous design against setup and hold constraints by propagating worst-case and best-case arrival times through the circuit graph, without simulating input vectors. *First defined in* [08-10](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-10-timing-metastability-cdc.md). *See also:* [Critical path](#critical-path), [Slack](#slack).

<a id="statistical-eye"></a>**Statistical eye** — An eye or bit-error estimate computed from a pulse response by enumerating (or convolving the distributions of) all interfering symbol patterns together with noise, rather than from a finite simulated record. *First defined in* [17-04](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-04-baseband-digital-transmission.md). *See also:* [Eye diagram](#eye-diagram).

<a id="statistical-independence"></a>**Statistical independence** — Events A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B), so learning one tells nothing about the other; several events are independent only if every subcollection satisfies the product rule. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="statistical-power"></a>**Statistical power** — The probability that a test rejects the null hypothesis when a specified alternative is true, 1 − β; it grows with sample size and effect size. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="statistical-process-control-spc"></a>**Statistical process control (SPC)** — Monitoring a process with control charts, plots of subgroup statistics against limits (typically ±3 standard errors around the grand mean), to detect drift or shifts; a process whose points stay inside the limits is "in statistical control". *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="status-flags"></a>**Status flags** — The Z (zero), N (negative, the result's sign bit), C (carry out) and V (signed overflow) bits produced by an ALU; unsigned A < B is a borrow (C = 0 after A − B) and signed A < B is N XOR V. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md).

<a id="steady-state-error"></a>**Steady-state error** — The error r − y that remains after the transient of a stable loop has died out, found with the final-value theorem as lim sE(s); it depends on the input class, the system type and where disturbances enter. *First defined in* [15-04](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-04-feedback-and-steady-state-error.md). *See also:* [Final-value theorem](#final-value-theorem).

<a id="steady-state-response"></a>**Steady-state response** — The part of a stable linear system's response that remains after the transient decays, set by the input alone; for a sinusoidal input it is the phasor answer. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Transient](#transient).

<a id="steep-slope-transistor"></a>**Steep-slope transistor** — A proposed switch, such as a tunneling FET or negative-capacitance FET, designed to turn on more sharply than the 59.5 mV/decade Boltzmann limit at 300 K by changing how carriers are injected; not yet a mainstream logic technology. *First defined in* [09-10](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-10-short-channel-effects-and-leakage.md).

<a id="steering-vector"></a>**Steering vector** — The vector of phase shifts a plane wave from angle θ produces across an antenna array, e^(−j2π(d/λ)k sin θ) for a uniform linear array; weighting by it points the beam at θ. *First defined in* [17-11](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-11-mimo-and-beamforming.md). *See also:* [Array factor](#array-factor), [Phased array](#phased-array).

<a id="steiner-tree"></a>**Steiner tree** — A tree connecting a net's pins that may add extra junctions (Steiner points). The rectilinear Steiner minimum tree is never longer than the minimum spanning tree, which is at most 3/2 times it; computing it exactly is NP-hard, so routers use heuristics. *First defined in* [19-11](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-11-place-route-signoff.md). *See also:* [Half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL)](#half-perimeter-wirelength-hpwl), [Maze routing](#maze-routing).

<a id="steinmetz-equation"></a>**Steinmetz equation** — The empirical core-loss fit P_v = k·f^α·B_pk^β for sinusoidal flux, with k, α and β fitted over a limited range of frequency, flux density and temperature. *First defined in* [22-05](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-05-magnetics-design.md). *See also:* [Core loss](#core-loss), [Improved generalized Steinmetz equation](#improved-generalized-steinmetz-equation).

<a id="step-coverage"></a>**Step coverage** — The ratio of film thickness on a feature's sidewall or bottom to that on the top surface; it falls with aspect ratio for transport-limited and line-of-sight processes. *First defined in* [25-03](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-03-deposition-etch-cmp-implant-metrology.md).

<a id="step-junction"></a>**Step junction** — A PN junction whose doping changes abruptly from N_A to N_D, with depletion width W = √(2ε(V_bi − V_A)(1/N_A + 1/N_D)/q). *First defined in* [09-05](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-05-pn-junction-electrostatics.md). *See also:* [One-sided junction](#one-sided-junction), [Linearly graded junction](#linearly-graded-junction).

<a id="step-response"></a>**Step response** — The response of a circuit to a source that switches from one constant value to another; for a first-order circuit, an exponential approach to the new final value. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="stepping"></a>**Stepping** — A silicon revision of a chip (e.g., A0, A1, B0); commonly the number changes for metal-only revisions and the letter for full-layer revisions, though conventions vary. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="stick-diagram"></a>**Stick diagram** — A dimensionless sketch of a cell's layout topology, with lines for active, polysilicon and metal and crossings of poly over active marking transistors, used to plan transistor ordering and wiring before drawing polygons. *First defined in* [19-09](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-09-layout-and-standard-cells.md). *See also:* [Euler path](#euler-path).

<a id="stiff-system"></a>**Stiff system** — A system of differential equations whose time constants span many orders of magnitude, so explicit methods need steps set by the fastest one; circuit simulators therefore use implicit methods. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Euler's method](#eulers-method).

<a id="stochastic-defects"></a>**Stochastic defects** — Random printing failures (rough edges, missing contacts, bridges) caused by Poisson fluctuations in the number of photons and reacting molecules per feature, worst in EUV because each photon carries 14 times the energy of a 193 nm photon. *First defined in* [25-02](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-02-lithography.md).

<a id="stokes-theorem"></a>**Stokes' theorem** — The circulation of a field around a closed loop equals the flux of its curl through any surface bounded by the loop; Green's theorem is its flat, two-dimensional case. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Curl](#curl).

<a id="stopband-attenuation"></a>**Stopband attenuation** — The minimum suppression a filter must give above its stopband edge, A_s = −20 log10 δs dB, where δs is the largest allowed stopband gain. *First defined in* [16-06](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-06-fir-filter-design.md). *See also:* [Passband ripple](#passband-ripple).

<a id="storage-capacitance"></a>**Storage capacitance** — The capacitance of a DRAM cell's capacitor, now below 10 fF; it sets the read signal and, with the cell's leakage, how long the cell retains data. *First defined in* [23-03](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-03-dram-cells-arrays-refresh.md). *See also:* [Transfer ratio](#transfer-ratio), [Retention time](#retention-time).

<a id="storage-time"></a>**Storage time** — The duration of the storage phase of reverse recovery, until the excess density at the junction edge reaches zero; exactly τ_p times the solution of erf√(t_s/τ_p) = I_F/(I_F + I_R) for a long diode, shorter than the charge-control estimate τ_p ln(1 + I_F/I_R). *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="storage-class-memory"></a>**Storage-class memory** — Memory meant to sit between DRAM and NAND in speed and cost, persistent like storage but byte-addressable; 3D XPoint (Optane) was the best-known attempt and was discontinued in 2021–2022. *First defined in* [23-08](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-08-emerging-memories.md). *See also:* [Phase-change memory (PCM)](#phase-change-memory-pcm).

<a id="store-buffer"></a>**Store buffer** — A queue that holds a core's retired stores until they are written to the cache, letting the core continue; its contents are visible to the core's own loads but not yet to other cores. *First defined in* [14-12](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-12-multicore-coherence-consistency.md). *See also:* [Total store ordering (TSO)](#total-store-ordering-tso).

<a id="straight-line-depreciation"></a>**Straight-line depreciation** — Spreading an asset's cost less salvage evenly over its life, D = (P − S)/n a year; depreciation is not a cash flow but lowers taxable income. *First defined in* [26-03](../courses/26-engineering-design-and-professional-practice/chapters/26-03-engineering-economics-1.md).

<a id="strained-silicon"></a>**Strained silicon** — Silicon whose lattice is deliberately stretched or compressed, by a SiGe substrate or by local stressors, to reshape its bands and raise carrier mobility; introduced into production logic processes at the 90 nm generation. *First defined in* [09-01](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-01-crystals-and-energy-bands.md).

<a id="streaming-multiprocessor-sm"></a>**Streaming multiprocessor (SM)** — The repeated core of an NVIDIA GPU, containing warp schedulers, arithmetic lanes, tensor cores, a large register file and shared memory; H100 has 132. *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [Graphics processing unit (GPU)](#graphics-processing-unit-gpu), [Occupancy](#occupancy).

<a id="strict-sense-stationary"></a>**Strict-sense stationary** — A random process whose every joint distribution of samples is unchanged by a common time shift; it implies wide-sense stationarity when the power is finite, and the two coincide for Gaussian processes. *First defined in* [17-01](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-01-random-processes-and-psd.md). *See also:* [Wide-sense stationary](#wide-sense-stationary), [Gaussian process](#gaussian-process).

<a id="strongarm-latch"></a>**StrongARM latch** — A clocked comparator with an input pair, NMOS and PMOS cross-coupled pairs and precharge switches; it draws no static current, gives rail-to-rail outputs, integrates the input difference with a gain of about (g_m/I_D) V_TH and then regenerates it with positive feedback. *First defined in* [20-05](../courses/20-analog-and-mixed-signal-ic-design/chapters/20-05-comparators-and-sample-and-hold.md). *See also:* [Regeneration time constant](#regeneration-time-constant), [Kickback](#kickback), [Metastability](#metastability).

<a id="struct-padding"></a>**Struct padding** — Unused bytes a compiler inserts between and after struct fields so that each field is aligned to its size; field order changes a struct's size (uint8, uint32, uint16 is 12 bytes; uint32, uint16, uint8 is 8). *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="structural-hazard"></a>**Structural hazard** — A pipeline hazard in which two instructions need the same hardware resource (a memory port, a register-file port, an unpipelined unit) in the same cycle. *First defined in* [14-06](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-06-pipelining-and-hazards.md).

<a id="structure-padding"></a>**Structure padding** — Unused bytes a compiler inserts between or after structure members so that each member sits at a multiple of its alignment; member order changes how much padding is needed. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md).

<a id="structured-sparsity"></a>**Structured sparsity** — A pruning pattern (such as 2:4, two zeros in every four weights) that tensor cores can exploit to skip zeros, doubling peak throughput; vendors' headline figures often assume it. *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [Tensor core](#tensor-core).

<a id="stub"></a>**Stub** — A short- or open-circuited length of transmission line used as a reactance, jZ₀ tan βℓ or −jZ₀ cot βℓ; short stubs act as inductors or capacitors at microwave frequencies where lumped parts misbehave. *First defined in* [13-08](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-08-transmission-lines-sinusoidal-steady-state.md). *See also:* [Input impedance](#input-impedance).

<a id="stuck-at-fault"></a>**Stuck-at fault** — A fault model in which one line (a gate output, primary input or fanout branch) is permanently 0 or 1; the single-stuck-at model, with one such fault at a time, is the basis of most production test generation. *First defined in* [19-12](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-12-design-for-test.md). *See also:* [Fault collapsing](#fault-collapsing), [Automatic test pattern generation (ATPG)](#automatic-test-pattern-generation-atpg).

<a id="student-t-distribution"></a>**Student t distribution** — The distribution of (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) for Gaussian data, with n − 1 degrees of freedom; heavier-tailed than the Gaussian, so small-sample intervals use larger multipliers (2.776 for ν = 4 at 95%). *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="subcarrier-spacing"></a>**Subcarrier spacing** — The frequency step Δf between OFDM subcarriers, equal to 1/T for a useful symbol of length T so that the subcarriers are orthogonal; NR uses 15·2^μ kHz (15 to 960 kHz). *First defined in* [17-10](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-10-ofdm.md). *See also:* [OFDM](#ofdm), [Numerology](#numerology).

<a id="subharmonic-oscillation"></a>**Subharmonic oscillation** — Alternating wide and narrow pulses at half the switching frequency in a peak current-mode converter above 50% duty cycle, caused by a current perturbation that grows by −m2/m1 each cycle. *First defined in* [22-07](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-07-converter-dynamics-and-control.md). *See also:* [Slope compensation](#slope-compensation).

<a id="subnet-mask-and-cidr"></a>**Subnet mask and CIDR** — A prefix length /p marks the first p bits of an IPv4 address as the network; a /p subnet holds 2^(32−p) − 2 usable hosts, and classless inter-domain routing aggregates contiguous prefixes into shorter ones. *First defined in* [17-13](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-13-computer-networks-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [Longest-prefix match](#longest-prefix-match).

<a id="subspace"></a>**Subspace** — A subset of a vector space that contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, such as a line or plane through the origin, a column space or a null space. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="substitution-integration"></a>**Substitution (integration)** — Evaluating ∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx as ∫ f(u) du with u = g(x), the chain rule in reverse; for definite integrals the limits change to g(a) and g(b). *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="substrate-pnp"></a>**Substrate PNP** — The vertical bipolar transistor available in any CMOS process (p⁺ diffusion emitter, n-well base, p-substrate collector); with its collector fixed at the substrate it is used diode-connected as the junction of CMOS bandgap references. *First defined in* [20-03](../courses/20-analog-and-mixed-signal-ic-design/chapters/20-03-bandgap-references.md). *See also:* [Bandgap reference](#bandgap-reference), [Bipolar junction transistor](#bipolar-junction-transistor).

<a id="subthreshold-conduction"></a>**Subthreshold conduction** — MOSFET current below threshold, carried by diffusion in a weak inversion layer and rising exponentially with gate voltage, I_D ∝ e^((V_GS − V_TH)/mV_T); it sets off-state leakage. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="subthreshold-logic"></a>**Subthreshold logic** — Digital logic run at a supply below the transistor thresholds, where current is exponential in the gate voltage; it minimizes energy per operation at low speed, and an inverter keeps gain down to a supply of 2(kT/q)ln(1 + n). *First defined in* [19-01](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-01-cmos-inverter-static.md). *See also:* [Subthreshold swing](#subthreshold-swing).

<a id="subthreshold-swing"></a>**Subthreshold swing** — The gate-voltage change per decade of subthreshold current, S = mV_T ln 10, which cannot fall below 59.5 mV/decade at 300 K for a conventional transistor. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="successive-approximation-sar-adc"></a>**Successive-approximation (SAR) ADC** — An ADC that holds its sample on a capacitor array doubling as a DAC and decides one bit per clock, most significant first, by comparing the DAC's output with the sample (a binary search); the usual converter on microcontrollers. *First defined in* [18-06](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-06-adc-dac-pwm.md). *See also:* [Sample-and-hold](#sample-and-hold), [Effective number of bits (ENOB)](#effective-number-of-bits-enob).

<a id="sufficient-statistic"></a>**Sufficient statistic** — A function of the observation that preserves all the information it holds about the hypothesis; in AWGN the correlator outputs onto the signal space's basis are sufficient, and the noise outside that space is irrelevant. *First defined in* [17-05](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-05-matched-filters-and-detection.md). *See also:* [Signal space](#signal-space).

<a id="sum-of-products-sop"></a>**Sum of products (SOP)** — An OR of AND terms; the canonical SOP ORs the minterms of the rows where the function is 1, and it maps onto two-level AND-OR or NAND-NAND logic. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md).

<a id="superheterodyne-receiver"></a>**Superheterodyne receiver** — A receiver that mixes the wanted signal with a tunable local oscillator to a fixed intermediate frequency (IF), where a fixed, sharp filter selects it; it must reject the image frequency before the mixer. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [Mixer](#mixer), [Image frequency](#image-frequency).

<a id="superjunction-mosfet"></a>**Superjunction MOSFET** — A silicon power MOSFET whose drift region is made of alternating p and n columns, beating silicon's unipolar on-resistance limit at 600–800 V at the cost of a very nonlinear output capacitance and large body-diode recovery charge. *First defined in* [22-06](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-06-converter-losses-and-wide-bandgap.md).

<a id="supermesh"></a>**Supermesh** — The loop around two meshes that share a current source, avoiding the source's branch; KVL around it does not involve the source's unknown voltage, and the source supplies the constraint i_a − i_b = ±I_s. *First defined in* [06-05](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-05-mesh-analysis.md). *See also:* [Supernode](#supernode), [Mesh analysis](#mesh-analysis).

<a id="supernode"></a>**Supernode** — A closed surface around a floating voltage source and its two nodes; KCL holds for the surface as a whole (the source's unknown current cancels), and the source supplies the constraint v_a − v_b = V_s. *First defined in* [06-04](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-04-nodal-analysis.md). *See also:* [Nodal analysis](#nodal-analysis).

<a id="superposition"></a>**Superposition** — In a linear circuit, any response to several independent sources equals the sum of the responses to each source acting alone, with the others switched off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened) and dependent sources left in place. It does not apply to power. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Linearity](#linearity), [Dependent source](#dependent-source).

<a id="superposition-electrostatics"></a>**Superposition (electrostatics)** — The principle that the field (or force) of many charges is the vector sum of their individual fields; for continuous charge the sum becomes an integral. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="superscalar"></a>**Superscalar** — A processor that fetches, decodes, issues and retires more than one instruction per cycle; its width is the maximum per cycle. *First defined in* [14-08](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-08-out-of-order-and-superscalar.md). *See also:* [Out-of-order execution](#out-of-order-execution).

<a id="surface-acoustic-wave-saw-filter"></a>**Surface acoustic wave (SAW) filter** — An acoustic filter in which interdigitated electrodes on a lithium tantalate or niobate surface launch and receive a surface wave; cheap and dominant below about 1 GHz, with temperature-compensated and multilayer variants extending it to about 2.7 GHz. *First defined in* [21-09](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-09-rf-front-end.md). *See also:* [Acoustic wave filter](#acoustic-wave-filter), [Temperature coefficient of frequency (TCF)](#temperature-coefficient-of-frequency-tcf).

<a id="surface-charge-density"></a>**Surface charge density** — Charge per unit area, σ (C/m²); on a conductor it is largest where the surface curves most sharply, and the field just outside is σ/ε₀. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="surface-depletion"></a>**Surface depletion** — The MOS bias regime in which majority carriers are pushed from the surface, leaving ionized dopants to a depth W_dep that grows with gate voltage until threshold. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="surface-mobility"></a>**Surface mobility** — The carrier mobility in a MOSFET inversion layer, several times below bulk mobility because of surface-roughness and phonon scattering, and falling as the vertical field rises. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="surface-potential"></a>**Surface potential** — The band bending φ_s at a semiconductor surface relative to the bulk, positive when the bands bend down; it is zero at flat band and reaches about 2φ_B at threshold in a MOS structure. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="surface-recombination-velocity"></a>**Surface recombination velocity** — The parameter S (cm/s) that sets recombination at a surface through the boundary condition D dΔp/dx = SΔp; 10² to about 10⁵ cm/s for bare silicon surfaces, below 1 cm/s at a well-passivated oxide interface. *First defined in* [09-04](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-04-generation-recombination-continuity.md).

<a id="surface-resistance"></a>**Surface resistance** — R_s = 1/(σδ) = √(πfµ/σ), the resistance per square of a conductor at high frequency (8.25 mΩ for copper at 1 GHz); the loss per area is ½R_s|H_t|², and it rises as √f. *First defined in* [13-05](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-05-plane-waves.md). *See also:* [Skin depth](#skin-depth).

<a id="surface-roughness-conductor"></a>**Surface roughness (conductor)** — The microscopic bumpiness of copper foil, which lengthens the current path once the skin depth falls to the bump size and multiplies conductor loss by up to about 2 (the Hammerstad–Jensen factor 1 + (2/π)arctan[1.4(Δrms/δ)²]). *First defined in* [24-01](../courses/24-high-speed-io-signal-integrity-and-photonics/chapters/24-01-signal-integrity-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [Skin effect](#skin-effect), [Insertion loss](#insertion-loss).

<a id="surge-impedance-loading-sil"></a>**Surge-impedance loading (SIL)** — The power V_LL²/Z_c a lossless line carries when terminated in its characteristic impedance; its series inductance then absorbs exactly the reactive power its capacitance generates, so the voltage is flat along the line. *First defined in* [22-12](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-12-power-systems-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [Characteristic impedance](#characteristic-impedance), [Ferranti effect](#ferranti-effect).

<a id="susceptance"></a>**Susceptance** — B, the imaginary part of an admittance (siemens); positive for a capacitor (ωC), negative for an inductor (−1/(ωL)). *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="sustained-power"></a>**Sustained power** — The largest power a product can dissipate indefinitely without exceeding a temperature limit, (T_max − T_ambient)/θ; short bursts can exceed it until the product's heat capacity fills. *First defined in* [27-01](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-01-system-analysis-method.md). *See also:* [Burst duration](#burst-duration), [Thermal time constant](#thermal-time-constant).

<a id="switch-figure-of-merit"></a>**Switch figure of merit** — The product R_DS(on)·Q (gate or output charge) of a switch technology, independent of device size; the minimum conduction-plus-charge loss is 2·I·√((RQ)·V·f_s), so a lower figure of merit allows a higher frequency. *First defined in* [22-06](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-06-converter-losses-and-wide-bandgap.md).

<a id="switch-figure-of-merit-ron-coff"></a>**Switch figure of merit (Ron·Coff)** — The product of an RF switch transistor's on-resistance and off-capacitance, in femtoseconds, independent of width and stack height; it fixes the trade between on-state loss and off-state isolation, with cut-off frequency 1/(2π R_on C_off). *First defined in* [21-09](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-09-rf-front-end.md). *See also:* [Transistor stacking](#transistor-stacking), [Silicon-on-insulator](#silicon-on-insulator).

<a id="switch-learning"></a>**Switch learning** — How an Ethernet switch builds its forwarding table, recording each frame's source MAC address against its arrival port and flooding frames to unknown destinations. *First defined in* [17-13](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-13-computer-networks-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [MAC address](#mac-address), [Ethernet frame](#ethernet-frame).

<a id="switch-node"></a>**Switch node** — The node of a switching converter that the power switches connect alternately to different voltages; its rectangular waveform carries the wanted average and the switching harmonics the filter must remove. *First defined in* [22-01](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-01-power-conversion-principles.md). *See also:* [Buck converter](#buck-converter).

<a id="switch-radix"></a>**Switch radix** — The number of ports a switch chip offers at a given port speed, its total bandwidth divided by the port rate; a two-tier leaf–spine fabric of radix-k switches connects k²/2 hosts at full bisection bandwidth. *First defined in* [24-05](../courses/24-high-speed-io-signal-integrity-and-photonics/chapters/24-05-pcie-cxl-ethernet.md). *See also:* [Leaf–spine fabric](#leaf-spine-fabric).

<a id="switch-stress"></a>**Switch stress** — A topology-comparison figure, the active switch's peak blocking voltage times its peak current divided by the output power; at D = 0.5 a buck or boost scores 2 and an inverting buck-boost 4. *First defined in* [22-03](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-03-boost-buck-boost-topologies.md). *See also:* [Buck-boost converter](#buck-boost-converter).

<a id="switched-capacitor-bank"></a>**Switched-capacitor bank** — A binary-weighted set of capacitors connected across a VCO tank by MOS switches, giving coarse digital tuning in overlapping bands so that the varactor, and the VCO gain, can stay small. *First defined in* [21-06](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-06-oscillators-and-vcos.md). *See also:* [Varactor](#varactor).

<a id="switched-capacitor-common-mode-feedback"></a>**Switched-capacitor common-mode feedback** — Common-mode feedback for clocked fully differential amplifiers in which capacitors sense the output common mode and a pair of switched capacitors, recharged every cycle to the desired offset, refresh them by charge sharing; it loads the outputs only capacitively and converges by the factor C_s/(C_s + C_r) per cycle. *First defined in* [20-02](../courses/20-analog-and-mixed-signal-ic-design/chapters/20-02-two-stage-op-amp-design.md). *See also:* [Common-mode feedback](#common-mode-feedback), [Fully differential amplifier](#fully-differential-amplifier).

<a id="switched-capacitor-converter"></a>**Switched-capacitor converter** — A converter that uses only switches and capacitors to move charge between voltage levels; its charge-sharing losses behave like an output resistance, R_eq = 1/(f·C) in the simplest case. *First defined in* [22-01](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-01-power-conversion-principles.md). *See also:* [Capacitor charging loss](#capacitor-charging-loss), [Charge pump](#charge-pump).

<a id="switching-converter"></a>**Switching converter** — A power converter built from switches and energy-storage elements (inductors, capacitors, transformers) that changes voltage and current at, ideally, constant power; ideal parts dissipate nothing, so its efficiency is limited only by real losses. *First defined in* [22-01](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-01-power-conversion-principles.md). *See also:* [Buck converter](#buck-converter), [Linear regulator](#linear-regulator), [DC transformer](#dc-transformer).

<a id="switching-energy"></a>**Switching energy** — The energy C·V² a supply delivers each time it charges a capacitance C from 0 to V; half is stored and half dissipated whatever the resistance, and the stored half is dissipated on discharge. With random data a wire draws C·V²/4 per bit. *First defined in* [23-01](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-01-memory-hierarchy-and-memory-wall.md). *See also:* [Energy per bit](#energy-per-bit).

<a id="switching-loss"></a>**Switching loss** — The energy a switch dissipates at each transition (overlap, output charge, reverse recovery) plus its gate-drive energy, multiplied by the switching frequency. *First defined in* [22-06](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-06-converter-losses-and-wide-bandgap.md). *See also:* [Overlap loss](#overlap-loss), [Output charge](#output-charge).

<a id="switching-threshold"></a>**Switching threshold** — The input voltage V_M at which a CMOS inverter's output equals its input; for square-law devices V_M = (V_TN√r + V_DD − |V_TP|)/(1 + √r) with r = k_n/k_p. *First defined in* [09-11](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-11-cmos-and-scaling.md).

<a id="symbol-rate"></a>**Symbol rate** — Symbols sent per second, 1/T, in baud; the bit rate is the symbol rate times log2 M, and the Nyquist frequency is half the symbol rate. *First defined in* [17-04](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-04-baseband-digital-transmission.md). *See also:* [Pulse-amplitude modulation](#pulse-amplitude-modulation), [Nyquist frequency](#nyquist-frequency).

<a id="symbolic-computation"></a>**Symbolic computation** — Manipulating formulas exactly, with symbols rather than numbers (SymPy solves, simplifies, differentiates and integrates); used to derive or check hand results and to keep exact rationals such as 470000/53. *First defined in* [05-03](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-03-scipy-sympy-matplotlib.md).

<a id="symmetrical-components"></a>**Symmetrical components** — Fortescue's decomposition of an unbalanced set of three phasors into balanced positive-, negative- and zero-sequence sets, each with its own network impedance, used to analyze unbalanced faults; a single-line-to-ground fault current is 3V/(Z1 + Z2 + Z0). *First defined in* [22-12](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-12-power-systems-fundamentals.md).

<a id="synchronizer"></a>**Synchronizer** — A chain of flip-flops (usually two or three) with nothing between them that samples an asynchronous signal and gives any metastability a clock period per stage to resolve; its reliability is quantified by MTBF = e^(S/tau)/(T_W F_C F_D). *First defined in* [08-10](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-10-timing-metastability-cdc.md). *See also:* [Metastability](#metastability), [Mean time between failures (MTBF)](#mean-time-between-failures-mtbf).

<a id="synchronous-counter"></a>**Synchronous counter** — A counter whose flip-flops all share one clock, each bit toggling when the bits below it say so (all 1s when counting up), so every output changes at the same edge. *First defined in* [08-07](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md). *See also:* [Ripple counter](#ripple-counter), [Modulo-N counter](#modulo-n-counter).

<a id="synchronous-design"></a>**Synchronous design** — A discipline in which all state is held in flip-flops clocked by a common clock, every feedback loop contains a register and asynchronous inputs are synchronized, so correctness reduces to setup and hold checks on each register-to-register path. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md).

<a id="synchronous-machine"></a>**Synchronous machine** — An AC machine whose rotor carries its own field (a DC winding or magnets) and turns at exactly synchronous speed; per phase it is an EMF E_f behind the synchronous reactance X_s. *First defined in* [22-11](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-11-electric-machines.md). *See also:* [Power angle](#power-angle), [Permanent-magnet synchronous machine (PMSM)](#permanent-magnet-synchronous-machine-pmsm).

<a id="synchronous-reactance"></a>**Synchronous reactance** — The per-phase reactance X_s of a synchronous machine that combines armature reaction and leakage; with the field EMF it sets the power–angle relation. *First defined in* [22-11](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-11-electric-machines.md).

<a id="synchronous-rectification"></a>**Synchronous rectification** — Replacing a converter's freewheeling diode with a controlled MOSFET, so the low-side drop is I·R_DS(on) instead of a forward voltage of about half a volt; essential at low output voltages, at the cost of a second driver and dead-time control. *First defined in* [22-02](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-02-buck-converter-steady-state.md). *See also:* [Dead time](#dead-time).

<a id="synchronous-reset"></a>**Synchronous reset** — A reset that is sampled like data and takes effect at the next active clock edge; simple to time but requires a running clock. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md). *See also:* [Asynchronous reset](#asynchronous-reset).

<a id="synchronous-speed"></a>**Synchronous speed** — The speed of an AC machine's rotating magnetic field, n_s = 120f/P rpm for P poles at frequency f; a synchronous machine's rotor turns at it, an induction machine's slightly slower. *First defined in* [22-11](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-11-electric-machines.md). *See also:* [Slip](#slip).

<a id="syndrome"></a>**Syndrome** — The vector s = rH^T computed from a received word; it equals eH^T for error pattern e, independent of the codeword sent, and indexes the most likely error to correct. *First defined in* [17-08](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-08-channel-coding.md). *See also:* [Parity-check matrix](#parity-check-matrix), [Hamming code](#hamming-code).

<a id="synopsys-design-constraints-sdc"></a>**Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC)** — The Tcl-based constraint format read by synthesis, timing and place-and-route tools: clock definitions, clock latency and uncertainty, input and output delays, port loads and drivers, and timing exceptions. *First defined in* [19-10](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-10-synthesis-and-sta.md). *See also:* [False path](#false-path), [Multicycle path](#multicycle-path), [Clock uncertainty](#clock-uncertainty).

<a id="synthesizable-subset"></a>**Synthesizable subset** — The part of an HDL that synthesis tools turn into hardware (continuous assignments, combinational and clocked always blocks, case, constant-bound loops, parameters); delays, system tasks, file I/O and most initial blocks are simulation-only. *First defined in* [08-05](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-05-verilog-and-testbenches.md).

<a id="system-signals-and-systems"></a>**System (signals and systems)** — A rule y = T{x} that maps a whole input signal to a whole output signal, such as a circuit, a filter, a channel or an algorithm; its properties (memory, linearity, time invariance, causality, stability, invertibility) decide which analysis tools apply. *First defined in* [11-02](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-02-system-properties.md). *See also:* [LTI system](#lti-system).

<a id="system-function"></a>**System function** — The eigenvalue of an LTI system for the exponential input, H(z) = Σ h[k]z^{−k} or H(s) = ∫ h(τ)e^{−sτ} dτ; for a constant-coefficient equation it is a ratio of polynomials whose denominator roots are the poles. *First defined in* [11-04](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-04-lti-systems-and-differential-equations.md).

<a id="system-noise-temperature"></a>**System noise temperature** — The sum of the antenna noise temperature and the receiver's equivalent noise temperature referred to the antenna terminals; the noise density there is N0 = k·Tsys. *First defined in* [17-02](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-02-noise-and-snr.md). *See also:* [Noise temperature](#noise-temperature), [Antenna noise temperature](#antenna-noise-temperature), [Carrier-to-noise-density ratio](#carrier-to-noise-density-ratio).

<a id="system-power-management-interface-spmi"></a>**System Power Management Interface (SPMI)** — A MIPI two-wire serial bus that links a phone or tablet SoC's power controller to one or more PMICs, so the SoC can change supply voltages and power states in real time. *First defined in* [22-08](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-08-pmics.md). *See also:* [Power-management IC (PMIC)](#power-management-ic-pmic).

<a id="system-type"></a>**System type** — The number N of integrators (poles at s = 0) in a loop gain L(s); type 0 leaves a finite error to a step, type 1 to a ramp, type 2 to a parabola. *First defined in* [15-04](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-04-feedback-and-steady-state-error.md). *See also:* [Static error constants](#static-error-constants).

<a id="system-in-package-sip"></a>**System-in-package (SiP)** — A package holding several dies and passive components that together form a complete subsystem, such as a wearable's processor, memory, power management and radio. *First defined in* [25-06](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-06-packaging-fundamentals.md).

<a id="system-level-cache-slc"></a>**System-level cache (SLC)** — A last-level cache shared by all the clients of an SoC (CPU, GPU, NPU, display, camera) in front of the DRAM controller; it cuts both DRAM bandwidth and the energy of memory accesses. *First defined in* [27-02](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-02-smartphone-soc.md). *See also:* [Application processor (AP)](#application-processor-ap).

<a id="system-level-test-slt"></a>**System-level test (SLT)** — Testing a packaged part by booting and running real software on an application-like board, catching timing-marginal and functional defects that structural tests miss. *First defined in* [25-11](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-11-test-ate-sort-burn-in.md).

<a id="systematic-offset"></a>**Systematic offset** — An offset that results from the design rather than from random mismatch, such as unequal drain voltages or a second stage whose current does not match its width ratio; it is the same on every chip and is removed by design, not by device area. *First defined in* [12-02](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-02-active-loads-cascodes-multistage.md). *See also:* [Input offset voltage](#input-offset-voltage), [Multistage amplifier](#multistage-amplifier).

<a id="systematic-yield"></a>**Systematic yield** — The yield factor from non-random losses (design-process interactions, parametric shifts, edge effects) that multiplies the random-defect yield. *First defined in* [25-04](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-04-yield-and-die-cost.md).

<a id="systemverilog"></a>**SystemVerilog** — The IEEE 1800 hardware design and verification language (current edition 1800-2023), a superset of Verilog adding the logic type, always_comb/always_ff, enums, assertions, classes, constrained randomization and coverage. *First defined in* [08-05](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-05-verilog-and-testbenches.md).

<a id="systemverilog-assertions-sva"></a>**SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)** — The temporal assertion language of IEEE 1800: clocked properties built from sequences (##n delays), implications (|-> and |=>) and system functions, used as assertions, assumptions or cover targets in simulation, formal tools and emulation. *First defined in* [19-13](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-13-verification-methods.md). *See also:* [SystemVerilog](#systemverilog), [Formal verification](#formal-verification).

<a id="systolic-array"></a>**Systolic array** — A grid of simple processing elements that pass operands to their neighbours each cycle, so that every value fetched at the edge is reused by a whole row or column; used for matrix multiplication in accelerators. *First defined in* [14-14](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-14-ai-accelerators.md). *See also:* [Processing element (PE)](#processing-element-pe), [Dataflow (accelerator)](#dataflow-accelerator).

<a id="letter-t"></a>

## T

<a id="t-flip-flop"></a>**T flip-flop** — A toggle flip-flop, Q⁺ = T ⊕ Q, which inverts its output at each clock edge when T = 1 and holds it when T = 0; a JK flip-flop with J = K = T behaves the same way. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md). *See also:* [JK flip-flop](#jk-flip-flop).

<a id="t-model"></a>**T model** — A small-signal transistor model with the emitter (or source) resistance r_e = α/g_m (1/g_m for a MOSFET) in the emitter lead and a controlled source αi_e from collector to the internal base; equivalent to the hybrid-π model and convenient when the emitter has series resistance. *First defined in* [10-04](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-04-small-signal-models.md). *See also:* [Hybrid-π model](#hybrid-model).

<a id="tag-cache"></a>**Tag (cache)** — The high-order address bits stored with each cache line, compared on a lookup to tell which of the memory blocks that map to the set is present. *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md). *See also:* [Cache block](#cache-block).

<a id="tail-current-source"></a>**Tail current source** — The current source feeding a differential pair's shared emitter or source node; its value sets the pair's total current and its output resistance sets the single-ended common-mode rejection. *First defined in* [12-01](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-01-differential-pairs.md). *See also:* [Differential pair](#differential-pair), [Common-mode gain](#common-mode-gain).

<a id="tail-chaining"></a>**Tail-chaining** — Starting the next pending exception handler directly when one returns, skipping the unstacking and restacking of registers (6 cycles instead of 12 + 12 on a Cortex-M3 or M4). *First defined in* [18-03](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-03-interrupts-exceptions-timers.md). *See also:* [Exception stack frame](#exception-stack-frame).

<a id="tanner-graph"></a>**Tanner graph** — The bipartite graph of a parity-check matrix, with a variable node per bit, a check node per parity equation and an edge per 1 in H; LDPC decoders pass messages along its edges. *First defined in* [17-08](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-08-channel-coding.md). *See also:* [LDPC code](#ldpc-code), [Belief propagation](#belief-propagation).

<a id="tape-out"></a>**Tape-out** — Releasing a chip's final layout database (GDSII or OASIS) to the foundry for mask making; the name comes from the magnetic tapes once used to deliver it. *First defined in* [19-11](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-11-place-route-signoff.md). *See also:* [Signoff](#signoff).

<a id="tapeout"></a>**Tapeout** — The milestone at which a chip's final design database is sent to manufacturing to make masks; after it, design changes require new masks and another fab cycle. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md). *See also:* [Respin](#respin).

<a id="target-impedance"></a>**Target impedance** — The highest impedance a power-delivery network may present to the load, V_DD × allowed ripple / current step; designers keep the network's impedance below it across frequency. *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Power delivery network](#power-delivery-network).

<a id="task-control-block-tcb"></a>**Task control block (TCB)** — The kernel's record of a task: its saved stack pointer, priority, state (ready, blocked, suspended) and the objects it waits for. *First defined in* [18-07](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-07-rtos-concepts.md). *See also:* [Context switch](#context-switch).

<a id="taylor-series"></a>**Taylor series** — f(x) = Σ f^(k)(a)(x − a)^k / k!, the power series matching every derivative of f at a (a Maclaurin series when a = 0). *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md). *See also:* [Lagrange remainder](#lagrange-remainder).

<a id="tbd-and-tbr"></a>**TBD and TBR** — To be determined (TBD) marks a requirement value that is unknown; to be resolved (TBR) marks a best estimate that still needs confirmation, with a rationale, an owner and a closing date. Counting open TBDs and TBRs is a simple measure of a specification's maturity. *First defined in* [26-01](../courses/26-engineering-design-and-professional-practice/chapters/26-01-requirements-and-specifications.md).

<a id="tcp"></a>**TCP** — The internet's reliable, in-order byte-stream transport, with a three-way handshake, sequence numbers and acknowledgements, flow control and AIMD congestion control. *First defined in* [17-13](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-13-computer-networks-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [Congestion window](#congestion-window), [Bandwidth-delay product](#bandwidth-delay-product), [UDP](#udp).

<a id="tcp-ip-model"></a>**TCP/IP model** — The four- or five-layer model the internet actually uses (link, internet, transport, application), folding OSI's session and presentation layers into the application. *First defined in* [17-13](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-13-computer-networks-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [OSI model](#osi-model).

<a id="tdma"></a>**TDMA** — Time-division multiple access, giving each user a recurring time slot in a frame, with guard times for timing error; usually combined with FDMA. *First defined in* [17-12](../courses/17-communication-systems/chapters/17-12-multiple-access-and-cellular-wifi.md). *See also:* [FDMA](#fdma), [OFDMA](#ofdma).

<a id="technology-mapping"></a>**Technology mapping** — The synthesis step that covers an optimized logic network with the cells of a target library (or with FPGA lookup tables), choosing covers that minimize area subject to timing constraints. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md).

<a id="technology-node"></a>**Technology node** — A generation of a fabrication process, historically shrinking features by about 0.7× (halving area) every two to three years; modern node names are labels, not physical lengths. *First defined in* [09-11](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-11-cmos-and-scaling.md).

<a id="telegraphers-equations"></a>**Telegrapher's equations** — The pair ∂v/∂z = −L′∂i/∂t − R′i and ∂i/∂z = −C′∂v/∂t − G′v for voltage and current on a transmission line, from the distributed model; for a TEM line they are Faraday's and Ampère–Maxwell's laws integrated across the cross-section. *First defined in* [13-07](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-07-transmission-lines-time-domain.md). *See also:* [Characteristic impedance](#characteristic-impedance), [Transmission line](#transmission-line).

<a id="telescopic-cascode-amplifier"></a>**Telescopic cascode amplifier** — A differential pair with cascode transistors stacked on its drains and cascode current-source loads, giving gain near (g_mr_o)²/2 in one stage at the cost of output swing, about V_DD minus five overdrives per side. *First defined in* [12-02](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-02-active-loads-cascodes-multistage.md). *See also:* [Cascode](#cascode), [Multistage amplifier](#multistage-amplifier).

<a id="tellegens-theorem"></a>**Tellegen's theorem** — In any lumped circuit the branch voltage–current products, with the passive sign convention, sum to zero; it follows from KCL and KVL alone, so it holds for nonlinear circuits and even across two circuits sharing a graph. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="temperature-coefficient-of-frequency-tcf"></a>**Temperature coefficient of frequency (TCF)** — The fractional drift of a resonator's frequency per degree, in ppm/°C; about −40 for plain lithium-tantalate SAW, −8 for multilayer SAW, about 27 in magnitude for AlN FBAR, and critical where a duplex gap is under 1 percent of the carrier. *First defined in* [21-09](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-09-rf-front-end.md). *See also:* [Duplex gap](#duplex-gap).

<a id="temperature-coefficient-of-resistance"></a>**Temperature coefficient of resistance** — The fractional change of resistance per degree, α in ρ = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]; 0.00393 /°C for annealed copper at 20 °C, negative for semiconductors and thermistors. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="tensor-arena"></a>**Tensor arena** — The block of SRAM a microcontroller inference library plans ahead of time for a network's activations and scratch buffers; its size is set by the largest set of tensors live at once, not by the sum over layers. *First defined in* [27-08](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-08-edge-ai-and-iot.md). *See also:* [TinyML](#tinyml).

<a id="tensor-core"></a>**Tensor core** — A GPU execution unit that performs a small matrix multiply-accumulate per instruction in low-precision formats, giving an order of magnitude more throughput than ordinary arithmetic lanes on matrix math. *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [Structured sparsity](#structured-sparsity).

<a id="tensor-parallelism"></a>**Tensor parallelism** — Splitting each layer's weight matrices across devices, which then exchange activations several times per layer on the critical path; it needs the bandwidth and latency of a scale-up fabric. *First defined in* [27-07](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-07-ai-datacenter-server-and-rack.md). *See also:* [Data parallelism](#data-parallelism), [Pipeline parallelism](#pipeline-parallelism), [Scale-up fabric](#scale-up-fabric).

<a id="termination-current"></a>**Termination current** — The tapering CV-phase charge current at which a charger declares the cell full and stops, typically a fraction of the fast-charge current. *First defined in* [22-09](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-09-batteries-charging-fuel-gauging.md).

<a id="tertiary-winding"></a>**Tertiary winding** — A third transformer winding, connected through a diode to the input, that returns a forward converter's magnetizing energy and resets its core; with N3 = N1 it limits the duty cycle to 0.5 and the switch voltage to 2·V_in. *First defined in* [22-04](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-04-isolated-converters.md). *See also:* [Forward converter](#forward-converter), [Core reset](#core-reset).

<a id="test-compression"></a>**Test compression** — On-chip decompressors that expand a few tester channels into many short internal scan chains, and compactors that fold their outputs back, cutting shift time and data by up to the ratio of internal chains to pins; realized test-time savings are smaller because of extra patterns, shift-speed limits and fixed per-die test steps. *First defined in* [19-12](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-12-design-for-test.md). *See also:* [Scan chain](#scan-chain), [Multiple-input signature register (MISR)](#multiple-input-signature-register-misr).

<a id="test-escape"></a>**Test escape** — A defective die that passes test; the escape rate among passing dies is (1 − Y)(1 − c)/[Y + (1 − Y)(1 − c)] for yield Y and coverage c, so it rises sharply when yield is low. *First defined in* [25-07](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-07-advanced-packaging-and-chiplets.md). *See also:* [Known-good die (KGD)](#known-good-die-kgd).

<a id="test-guard-band"></a>**Test guard band** — A margin added to a test limit to allow for measurement error; widening it reduces escapes but increases overkill and pushes parts into lower bins. *First defined in* [25-11](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-11-test-ate-sort-burn-in.md). *See also:* [Overkill](#overkill).

<a id="test-source"></a>**Test source** — A voltage or current source applied at a port, with all independent sources turned off but dependent sources left in place, to find the resistance seen there as v_t/i_t. *First defined in* [06-06](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-06-dependent-sources.md). *See also:* [Dependent source](#dependent-source).

<a id="testbench"></a>**Testbench** — Simulation-only code that instantiates a design, applies inputs and checks outputs; the executable form of a design's specification. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md). *See also:* [Self-checking testbench](#self-checking-testbench).

<a id="thermal-budget"></a>**Thermal budget** — The cumulative time-at-temperature a wafer sees after a given step; it limits later processing because dopants keep diffusing and sensitive materials (metal gates, copper, low-k films) degrade when heated. *First defined in* [25-01](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-01-process-flow-overview.md).

<a id="thermal-capacitance"></a>**Thermal capacitance** — The heat a body stores per kelvin of temperature rise, C_th = mc (J/K); the thermal analogue of a capacitor to ground. *First defined in* [15-01](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-01-modeling-dynamic-systems.md). *See also:* [Thermal resistance](#thermal-resistance).

<a id="thermal-design-power-tdp"></a>**Thermal design power (TDP)** — The sustained power a cooling solution must be designed to remove for a chip; definitions differ by vendor (NVIDIA's per-GPU TDP, AMD's typical board power), so boundaries must be checked before comparing. *First defined in* [25-08](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-08-thermal-engineering.md). *See also:* [Junction temperature](#junction-temperature).

<a id="thermal-impedance"></a>**Thermal impedance** — Z_th(t), the temperature rise per watt in response to a power step; it rises from near zero for very short pulses to the steady thermal resistance, and datasheets give it as a Foster RC network. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md). *See also:* [Foster network](#foster-network), [Cauer network](#cauer-network), [Thermal resistance](#thermal-resistance).

<a id="thermal-interface-material-tim"></a>**Thermal interface material (TIM)** — A thin layer (grease, pad, phase-change material, solder or liquid metal) between a die and its lid, or a lid and its cooler, that fills microscopic gaps; its low conductivity makes even a 25 µm layer a major thermal resistance. *First defined in* [25-08](../courses/25-fabrication-packaging-test-and-reliability/chapters/25-08-thermal-engineering.md). *See also:* [Thermal resistance](#thermal-resistance).

<a id="thermal-noise"></a>**Thermal noise** — Johnson–Nyquist noise of a resistor at temperature T, white and Gaussian with one-sided density 4kTR (V²/Hz); 4.07 nV/√Hz for 1 kΩ at 300 K. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="thermal-resistance"></a>**Thermal resistance** — R_th (K/W), the temperature rise per watt of heat flowing along a path; with heat capacity C_th it forms a thermal time constant R_th C_th, the thermal analog of an RC circuit. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="thermal-runaway"></a>**Thermal runaway** — Positive feedback in which rising temperature raises power dissipation (for example leakage), which raises temperature further; it runs away when the loop gain R_th·dP/dT reaches 1. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Thermal resistance](#thermal-resistance).

<a id="thermal-runaway-battery"></a>**Thermal runaway (battery)** — A self-accelerating failure in which heat from a cell's exothermic decomposition reactions raises its temperature and speeds the reactions, leading to venting, fire or explosion; triggered by overcharge, overheating, damage or an internal short. *First defined in* [22-09](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-09-batteries-charging-fuel-gauging.md). *See also:* [Battery protection circuit](#battery-protection-circuit).

<a id="thermal-stability-factor"></a>**Thermal stability factor** — Δ = E_b/k_BT, an MRAM free layer's energy barrier in units of thermal energy; a bit flips at about f₀e^(−Δ), so an N-bit array held for time t needs Δ ≳ ln(N t f₀). *First defined in* [23-08](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-08-emerging-memories.md). *See also:* [Spin-transfer torque (STT)](#spin-transfer-torque-stt).

<a id="thermal-throttling"></a>**Thermal throttling** — Limiting a chip's power, usually through DVFS, to keep its junction temperature below a limit; the controller (typically a clamped PI) holds the temperature at the limit while the permitted power decays from a burst level to the sustained level with the heat sink's time constant. *First defined in* [15-12](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-12-control-applications-pll-regulators-thermal.md). *See also:* [Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)](#dynamic-voltage-and-frequency-scaling-dvfs), [Thermal resistance](#thermal-resistance).

<a id="thermal-time-constant"></a>**Thermal time constant** — The product of thermal resistance and thermal capacitance, τ = θC_th, which sets how fast a body's temperature approaches its steady value after a change in power. *First defined in* [27-01](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-01-system-analysis-method.md). *See also:* [Sustained power](#sustained-power).

<a id="thermal-velocity"></a>**Thermal velocity** — The root-mean-square speed of carriers from thermal energy, √(3kT/m\*), about 2.3×10⁷ cm/s for electrons in silicon at 300 K; drift is a small bias on this random motion. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md).

<a id="thermal-voltage"></a>**Thermal voltage** — V_T = kT/q, the voltage scale of thermal energy per unit charge; about 25.85 mV at 300 K. It sets the ~60 mV/decade slope of diode and subthreshold transistor currents. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="thermionic-emission"></a>**Thermionic emission** — Current carried by carriers energetic enough to pass over a barrier, J = KT²e^(−qφ_B/kT)(e^(qV/kT) − 1) for a Schottky diode; it involves only majority carriers. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md). *See also:* [Richardson constant](#richardson-constant).

<a id="thermo-compression-bonding-with-non-conductive-film-tc-ncf"></a>**Thermo-compression bonding with non-conductive film (TC-NCF)** — An HBM stacking method that bonds each die under heat and pressure through a non-conductive film; lower thermal resistance than MR-MUF but sensitive to die warpage. *First defined in* [23-05](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-05-hbm-in-depth.md). *See also:* [Mass reflow molded underfill (MR-MUF)](#mass-reflow-molded-underfill-mr-muf), [Hybrid bonding](#hybrid-bonding).

<a id="thermomechanical-noise"></a>**Thermomechanical noise** — The random force 4kTb (N²/Hz) that the damping gas exerts on a mechanical structure, the twin of a resistor's 4kTR; it sets an accelerometer's noise floor √(4kTω₀/(mQ)). *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="thermometer-code"></a>**Thermometer code** — The pattern of comparator outputs in a flash ADC, all ones below the input level and all zeros above it; an isolated wrong bit is called a bubble. *First defined in* [20-07](../courses/20-analog-and-mixed-signal-ic-design/chapters/20-07-nyquist-adcs.md). *See also:* [Flash ADC](#flash-adc).

<a id="thevenin-equivalent"></a>**Thevenin equivalent** — A voltage source V_th (the open-circuit voltage) in series with R_th, equivalent at two terminals to any linear network; R_th is found with independent sources switched off and dependent sources kept. *First defined in* [06-08](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-08-thevenin-and-norton.md). *See also:* [Norton equivalent](#norton-equivalent), [Thevenin resistance](#thevenin-resistance), [Open-circuit voltage](#open-circuit-voltage).

<a id="thevenin-resistance"></a>**Thevenin resistance** — R_Th, the resistance seen looking into two terminals of a linear circuit with its independent sources turned off; it sets the time constant seen by a capacitor or inductor connected there. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="third-order-intercept-point-ip3"></a>**Third-order intercept point (IP3)** — The extrapolated power at which the third-order intermodulation products of two equal tones, growing 3 dB per dB, would equal the fundamental, growing 1 dB per dB; quoted at the input (IIP3) or output (OIP3) and measured as IIP3 = Pin + (Pfund − PIM3)/2. *First defined in* [21-03](../courses/21-rf-and-microwave-engineering/chapters/21-03-noise-figure-and-linearity.md). *See also:* [Intermodulation distortion](#intermodulation-distortion), [P1dB (1 dB compression point)](#p1db-1-db-compression-point), [Second-order intercept point (IP2)](#second-order-intercept-point-ip2).

<a id="third-quadrant-conduction"></a>**Third-quadrant conduction** — Reverse conduction of a GaN HEMT, which has no body diode, at a voltage drop that depends on its off-state gate voltage; it has no recovery charge but can cost more per nanosecond of dead time. *First defined in* [22-06](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-06-converter-losses-and-wide-bandgap.md).

<a id="thrashing"></a>**Thrashing** — The collapse in performance when a program's working set exceeds the available physical frames, so that nearly every access causes a page fault. *First defined in* [14-10](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-10-virtual-memory.md). *See also:* [Demand paging](#demand-paging).

<a id="threat-model"></a>**Threat model** — A statement of what must be protected (assets), from whom (attackers with their access, skill and budget) and through which entry points (attack surfaces), used to choose and justify security mechanisms. *First defined in* [18-11](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-11-hardware-security.md). *See also:* [Root of trust](#root-of-trust).

<a id="three-cs-compulsory-capacity-conflict"></a>**Three Cs (compulsory, capacity, conflict)** — A classification of cache misses into compulsory (first access to a block), capacity (the working set exceeds the cache, so a fully associative cache of the same size also misses) and conflict (too many blocks map to one set). *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md). *See also:* [Miss rate](#miss-rate).

<a id="three-phase-system"></a>**Three-phase system** — AC power as three sinusoidal voltages of equal amplitude 120° apart; a balanced three-phase load draws constant instantaneous power, needs 75% of the copper of single phase for the same power and loss, and produces rotating fields for motors. *First defined in* [07-11](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-11-three-phase-circuits.md).

<a id="threshold-gain"></a>**Threshold gain** — The material gain at which a laser's round-trip gain equals its losses, g_th = α_i + (1/2L) ln(1/R₁R₂); above it the laser oscillates. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="threshold-roll-off"></a>**Threshold roll-off** — The fall of threshold voltage as channel length shrinks, because the source and drain help lower the channel barrier; in Hu's model ΔV_TH = (V_DS + 0.4 V) e^(−L/l_d). *First defined in* [09-10](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-10-short-channel-effects-and-leakage.md).

<a id="threshold-switching"></a>**Threshold switching** — The electronic (not structural) switch of an amorphous chalcogenide into a conducting state above a threshold voltage, which lets a high-resistance PCM cell pass programming current. *First defined in* [23-08](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-08-emerging-memories.md). *See also:* [Phase-change memory (PCM)](#phase-change-memory-pcm), [Selector (memory)](#selector-memory).

<a id="threshold-voltage"></a>**Threshold voltage** — The gate voltage at which a MOS surface becomes inverted, conventionally where the surface electron density equals the body doping, V_TH = V_FB + 2φ_B + √(2qN_Aε_s 2φ_B)/C_ox; foundries define it by a drain current. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="threshold-voltage-drift"></a>**Threshold-voltage drift** — A slow shift of a SiC MOSFET's gate threshold under gate and switching stress over its life, which mainly raises its on-resistance; managed by the gate-drive voltage window. *First defined in* [22-06](../courses/22-power-electronics-and-energy-conversion/chapters/22-06-converter-losses-and-wide-bandgap.md).

<a id="through-silicon-via-tsv"></a>**Through-silicon via (TSV)** — A copper pillar through a thinned silicon die, insulated by an oxide liner, that carries signals and power vertically through a die stack; electrically a short wire of about a hundred femtofarads, physically costly in area and process steps. *First defined in* [23-05](../courses/23-memory-and-storage-technology/chapters/23-05-hbm-in-depth.md). *See also:* [TSV keep-out zone](#tsv-keep-out-zone), [High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)](#high-bandwidth-memory-hbm).

<a id="throughput"></a>**Throughput** — The amount of work completed per unit time (tasks per second, operations per second), as distinct from latency, the time one task takes. *First defined in* [14-01](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-01-performance-power-iron-law.md). *See also:* [Latency](#latency).

<a id="throughput-interactivity-frontier"></a>**Throughput–interactivity frontier** — The tradeoff between a serving system's total tokens per second and each user's tokens per second as the batch grows; in the memory-bound region it is a straight line whose slope is the ratio of weight bytes to one sequence's KV-cache bytes. *First defined in* [27-07](../courses/27-system-architectures/chapters/27-07-ai-datacenter-server-and-rack.md). *See also:* [KV cache](#kv-cache), [Decode and prefill](#decode-and-prefill).

<a id="thumb-2"></a>**Thumb-2** — Arm's mixed 16- and 32-bit instruction encoding, the only instruction set of Cortex-M cores; Armv6-M implements a mostly 16-bit subset, Armv7-M and later the full set. *First defined in* [18-01](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-01-microcontroller-architecture.md). *See also:* [Microcontroller](#microcontroller).

<a id="tickless-idle"></a>**Tickless idle** — Stopping an RTOS's periodic tick while no task is due, and reprogramming a timer for the next deadline, so the MCU can stay in a low-power state longer. *First defined in* [18-07](../courses/18-embedded-systems-and-microcontrollers/chapters/18-07-rtos-concepts.md). *See also:* [Real-time operating system (RTOS)](#real-time-operating-system-rtos).

<a id="time-aliasing"></a>**Time aliasing** — The folding of a sequence onto itself every N samples, x̃[n] = Σ x[n + rN], when its DTFT is sampled at only N frequencies; absent when the sequence is no longer than N. *First defined in* [16-03](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-03-the-dft.md). *See also:* [Aliasing (sampling)](#aliasing-sampling).

<a id="time-borrowing"></a>**Time borrowing** — In latch-based (for example two-phase) design, a slow half-cycle's data passing through a transparent latch and using time from the next half-cycle; up to T_c/2 − t_setup may be borrowed with a 50% duty cycle. *First defined in* [19-07](../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-07-sequential-timing-and-clocking.md). *See also:* [Sequencing overhead](#sequencing-overhead).

<a id="time-constant"></a>**Time constant** — τ, the characteristic time of a first-order exponential response e^{−t/τ}; τ = R_Th·C for an RC circuit and τ = L/R_Th for an RL circuit. After one τ, 63.2 % of the change is complete. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md). *See also:* [Thevenin resistance](#thevenin-resistance), [Settling time](#settling-time).
